speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister referred to the reforms as an experiment and that he was going to monitor the progress, the weaknesses and the strengths of them. Would he agree to have an ongoing review process put in place now? If somebody in the House felt strongly about certain amendments to our rules not working properly, could we appeal the case to somebody, grieve it to somebody in the House, either the Privileges and Elections Committee or some other committee so that we could get satisfaction? I am thinking particularly of legislative committees that for a number of months have been proliferating. We have no way of going to anybody to make sure that the legislative committees were queued or put in order by the House. Would the Minister answer that question please?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) raises a very important question. Let me respond in two ways. With respect to the precise matter of legislative committees, the Hon. Member will be aware that in the first report, the recommendations of which were accepted, that legislative committees were to consist of between 20 and 30 members. Our experience showed that this put enormous pressure on the Hon. Member who is the whip of the Official Opposition. He has a sense of this as much as anyone, and I know from speaking with the other two whips that this has put pressures on in terms of serving on those committees in a meaningful way. I have talked with members of the committee, including the chairman, who indicates that what was intended and what we have accepted in this set of revisions is that there be no minimum number of members for legislative committees. The striking committee will assess each topic. The number of members on legislative committees will depend on the relative importance of the legislation.
Accordingly, it may be appropriate for certain pieces of legislation to have by way of example seven members on a committee, whereas other topics may be of such crucial importance that we want to get a committee made up of over 20 members.
With respect to the Member's observation of monitoring and the method by which the rules can be dealt with and grievances or points of view put forward, I believe that with the present regime of rules, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has that very function. It would be my suggestion that this is an ongoing reference which they will now have under the new rules. We will now make a permanent reference with respect to these matters, including the whole question and rules of the House to the committee.
This committee will become very important as it is the vehicle for which all members, regardless on which side of the House they sit, will be able to put forward their suggestions and recommendations, have a thorough hearing and report and make a recommendation back to the House.
I have discussed this matter-not with any amount of thoroughness, but the matter has been discussed and I think it is fair for me to reveal that some of the discussions took place with House leaders. It seems to me that might be an appropriate thing for all Parties to be involved in, to look at the process a to make sure the legislative committees are working efficiently.

Mr. Speaker, in general I think the proposals for Private Members' Business are good, but I am still somewhat concerned about the suggested process for selecting private Members' Bills for voting. According to the proposed new Standing Orders, there would be a standing committee on Private Members' Business which would meet and select from the Private Members' Bills and motions on the Order Paper six that would be votable, and go through a special process. In principle that is good, but I am concerned about how it might work in practice.
February 11, 1986

First, the majority on that committee will be from the Government side, no matter what Parliament we are in. The majority can decide not to bring in any Bills or motions for a vote which might affect the Government, or might try to avoid any kind of controversial legislation, so that we would just vote upon very bland Bills.
I should like to refer to my Bill as an example, and not ask for any opinion on it. I am referring to Bills such as the one I have had for many years on gun control. In fact, the matter was raised yesterday by a Government Member. How do we see any possibility of Bills dealing with subjects such as that getting through a committee on Private Members' Business? Does the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) think that process will be one where we vote on bland Bills, as we did in the past, such as the one to make the beaver the national animal of Canada, or the one by which the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) was successful in changing the name of Trans-Canada Airlines to Air Canada? 1 think those were good things, but I hope the process will be advanced further than that. Could the President of the Privy Council assure us that the process will give the House an opportunity to bring to a vote Bills of some significance?
I understand that the Government must protect itself but, for this process to be meaningful, the committee has to deal with matters in a somewhat objective way so that we have a chance to discuss and vote upon Bills which will have some meaning.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from that point of view, the recommendations absolutely follow the recommendations of the special committee on reform which was chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East. In the matter of Private Members' Business, we have tried to reflect accurately, with one exeption, the recommendations of that committee. We are talking about Private Members' Business. Parliament consists of representatives of various political Parties. However, in terms of Private Members' Business, it will reflect the membership of the House from time to time in subsequent Parliaments.
The two representations I have received have been at opposite ends of the spectrum, quite frankly. One was made by the Hon. Member, that we make sure significant items are allowed to come forward. I believe that we will have a chance to see, in this period of provisional application, private Members in control of their own destiny, not influenced by and not having the participation of Government Members, shall we say. They will exercise their judgment, to the benefit of private Members. That is the whole purpose of this kind of private Members' control over the agenda.
The other stream of representations I have received is a concern that somehow matters of great significance will in fact be dealt with in Private Members' Hour. This is the dilemma one faces; we have to make up our minds. Either private Members will be able to bring forward issues of importance or not. I opt for that. My position is that Private Members' Business will not be mere puffery, but I am only one Member among 282.
Standing Orders
The Hon. Member's question is a valid one. There has been a suggestion that perhaps there would be an opportunity to steamroll things through Private Members' Hour. I do not think that is a valid argument now, because we have not allowed for the telescoping of the debate. We have also extended the time available for private Members to participate in important issues. There will be 10-minute speeches and virtually an opportunity for all private Members to participate on really significant issues. I think we have reached a very satisfactory accord in respect of Private Members' Business. I am very interested to see how it will work. Notwithstanding my own views in respect of the Hon. Member's proposed legislation, I see no problem in that matter being debated fully and being put to a vote. I do not see how that would offend anyone's sensibilities. He may not be successful on a vote, but at least it would be put to a vote.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering this debate I do not want to begin by dealing with the specific proposals for procedural changes which are before us, but generally with the purposes of parliamentary reform. Our object in considering reform ought not to be merely for the purpose of attempting to keep some Members who feel underemployed busy, or to make some Members feel that their work is somehow more meaningful. Our object should not be to make Parliament either an automatic legislative mill or, at the extremity, a mere cockpit for partisan political posturing. Our object must be to seek to make Parliament do better that which it is intended to do.
Parliament is here to consider and make final decisions on legislative proposals and, in doing so, to have the opportunity to alter and present alternatives to such proposals. However, the reality is that when we talk about legislative proposals, we are, to all intents and purposes, talking about those presented by the Government. Only the Government, that is the Ministry, can propose legislation to spend money or requiring the expenditure of money to achieve its purposes. Most of the time for debate is reserved for measures the Government wishes to introduce. The package before us does not change any of these essential facts.
This is consistent with the basic principle of parliamentary Government, that of responsibility. The Government is formed by those having the support of the largest number of Members. This means, with rare exceptions, that the Government is formed by the Party having the largest number of seats in the House, the largest number of Members. That Government must take responsibility for its actions or non-action to Parliament and, through Parliament, to the Canadian people between elections and ultimately directly to the Canadian people which makes decisions on whether a Party forming a Government should continue or be replaced by one of the other Parties in a general election.
Therefore, it could be argued that Parliament's function in our democratic system is primarily to hold Governments to account on behalf of the Canadian people in the broadest sense of the term. If that is the case, then we are talking about having Parliament in a position to examine every action of

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
Government and to provide Government with a framework for operation which meets the needs and expectations of the Canadian people. I submit that everything Parliament does- legislation, examination of the Estimates and seeking information-flows from this basic concept. Surely we must examine all our procedures and all proposals for changes in those procedures in this context.
From what I have said, I think it is clear that we must examine any proposal for change, for reform of Parliament, in the context of our system of political Parties. Our parliamentary system is not simply one of Government and private Members, those Members who form the Government and those who do not.
To suggest this, and there is a disturbing flavour of this in the Government's proposals to change the Standing Orders, overlooks the reality of our parliamentary system, what it is and what I believe it should be. We do not talk of a system of checks and balances in our legislative, executive and judicial structures in the same way as the Americans do. Perhaps, in a more subtle and limited sense, we do have a system with checks and balances here in Canada and in our Parliament, our House of Commons. The balance, the creative tensions in that system are not simply those between the Government and Private Members. They are between Government, that is the Party forming the Government, and the other Parties as well. This is recognized, particularly by the fact that both in law and in parliamentary practice and precedent, the concept of the Official Opposition is enshrined; that is the Party with the second largest number of seats. We have gone even further here in this House of Commons and have recognized formally the position of other Parties if they have a minimum number of seats.
An essential feature of our Canadian parliamentary system-essential to our own Canadian approach to checks and balances-is the existence of parties other than the one forming the Government and their ability, particularly that of the party forming the Official Opposition, to play an active and meaningful role. What happens if that system, even in a well meaning and inadvertent way, is tilted so that this concept of parties testing one another and vying for support through their challenges to Government, alternatives, ideas and people on the one hand, and the Government putting forward its proposals on the other hand, is weakened? Then I say Parliament is weakened and the risks of untested, unchecked and, therefore, bad government is dangerously increased.
Parliament is not simply Government and private Members, it is, particularly today, the Party forming the Government and those Parties in opposition to it. It is clear we must examine any proposals for parliamentary reform in the context of the party system.
Over the years, Parliament has structured all of its activities around the parliamentary system. Constitutionally, most legislative initiatives are in the hands of the Ministry, those who are supported by the Party with the largest number of members. In turn, the Ministry organizes its supporters in the House of Commons in such a way so as to maintain their support, therefore, the confidence of the House, and to see its legislative initiatives acted upon. In order to hold the Government to account and to scrutinize its proposals. The Opposition as well has to be organized in particular ways.
The House, in any process or decision of reform, must ensure it has procedures that facilitate the organization, not only of the Government and its supporters, but of the Opposition as well. Our electoral system reflects this kind of organization. Study after scholarly study shows that the overwhelming majority of the Canadian electorate makes its choice at the polls, to a large degree, on the basis of political party and leadership. While each elector votes individually for an individual member, his or her decision is heavily influenced by party considerations. Candidates are mostly chosen by party processes. Elections are basically conducted on a party basis, and almost every member is elected, whether or not we admit it to ourselves as individuals, largely for party reasons.
Thus when we reach the House of Commons we face a dual situation. We have 282 individual members elected from what are still 282 separate districts. We also have a system that is organized into Government and opposition for the purpose of carrying on the business of Parliament. Both these facts must be reconciled, in the organization of the House and its rules, and if we are to fulfil the expectations of our electors we must bear them in mind.
Having said this, I do not want to be understood to be downgrading in any way the role of the individual Member of Parliament. The people, in making party choices, clearly do not wish their elected representatives to be trained seals functioning only as instruments of their parties, they expect initiative and individual participation to the fullest. Our party system, indeed, depends upon these very qualities for its vitality.
A major factor in the role played by individual Members, the major way in which they have an impact either on the proposals or actions of the Government, or of their party if it is not the one forming the Government, is through something not recognized in the Standing Orders at all, but which is very real all the same. I refer to the party caucuses and the caucus committees.
Bearing all this in mind, I want to make some comments on the Government's proposals. These proposals are, of course, not exactly those made by the Special Committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), who are intimately involved in the proceedings of that committee, will be commenting more extensively on this. I want to say that all the Members of the committee worked both intensively and extensively and are to be congratulated for the production of their very comprehensive and challenging reports. The proposals now before us are in fact the initiatives of the Government. The report of the committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was the taking off
February 11, 1986

point, but the proposals are in many places quite different than the committee's recommendations.
I want to say in this regard that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has talked with myself and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), as the House Leaders of our respective Parties, about the Government's proposals and he has taken into account a number of our suggestions. This has likely made possible a debate that would be easier and more positive than would otherwise be the case at this time, but there remain a number of considerations for the House before it reaches any decision.
I want to stress that there has been no package deal worked out behind the scenes to simply whiz this measure through without any real debate. The debate today, as far as I and the members of the Official Opposition are concerned is to go on here on the floor of the House of Commons into the pros and cons of the Government's proposal. This is not simply a pro forma gesture aimed at enshrining something worked out behind the scenes. I want to say the individual Member rightly expects to be active and to count for more than simply casting his or her vote at the direction of his or her party whip.
The individual Member rightly expects to be active and to count in the visible workings of Parliament, to take part in a more visible and meaningful way. I recognize and support the importance of their work as individual Members of Parliament. Therefore, we must consider the effect of the proposed changes of the rules on both aspects of a member's work, as someone who is a member of a party caucus and as someone who has an individual standing and is directly elected for a particular constituency.
Therefore, it is important in this debate today, and subsequently, if necessary, that we hear from individual Members of Parliament, particularly those not on the government side, whether they feel the Government's proposed changes in the rules actually improve or retard their ability to do their work as they see it. My approach, and that of the Official Opposition to this debate, is one which is sympathetic to parliamentary reform. However, our members want to discuss openly here in the House of Commons the extent to which the Government's proposed changes in the rules do, in fact, bring reform in the sense of enabling them to do their work in a more vigorous and effective way.
Last June, acting on the basis of the Special Committee's initial recommendations, a number of provisional revisions to the Standing Orders were adopted. Some of these have caused many individual MPs from both the Government and Opposition sides great concern. One problem arises from the decision to do the committee stage of consideration of legislation in legislative committees rather than in Standing Committees. This has led to an incredible proliferation of committees and committee meetings, placing an almost impossible burden on Members wishing to specialize in particular subjects. It is not an infrequent occurrence that meetings of more than one legislative committee or of a Standing Committee considering
Standing Orders
matters falling within the same general subject area are held at the same time or so close in time to one another that Members concerned are either physically unable to attend meetings or to prepare themselves properly for meetings. It has also happened that the subject under consideration in the House has conflicted with committee consideration; this situation cannot continue.
If the Government wants to enhance the role of the individual MP, I do not think continuing this proliferation of legislative committees and meetings is the way to do it. The private Member of Parliament needs time to reflect, to prepare and to talk to individuals and groups concerned with the subject matter being looked at in committees on which that Member serves. This cannot take place if there are so many committee meetings that the MP is spending all his time at meetings or running from one to the other. To do real committee work the Member must have available to him adequate time for preparation, reflection and contact with the public. The Member also needs time to be able to participate in debate in the House itself, take part in the work of his caucus, attend to the problems of his constituency and meet with interest groups or individuals that want to meet with that Member.
In the United Kingdom only a fixed, a limited number of legislative committees may sit at one time. There are only so many queues or slots for those committees. As a result, Bills are apportioned and scheduled to legislative committees whose meetings are set up so as to minimize conflicts for Members. Some adaption of this queue system will have to be put in place here if the system is to have a chance to work and continue.
Frankly, this is a problem that was not anticipated when the provisional rules were adopted last June, but unless some correction is made that is satisfactory to Opposition Parties, the difficulties that have arisen threaten the continuance of the whole procedural package or the adoption of further changes.
I will have more to say about the proposals regarding committees and the motion before us, but before leaving this point I would also like to say that for any new proposals to be adopted the Government must make a formal commitment right now that it will be willing to join with the Opposition Parties in making adjustments from time to time during the 10-month experimental life of any changes proposed should further unforeseen problems arise. Yes, the Government's proposals are for an experimental period of only 10 months, but we also know too well that even one week is a long time in politics. The commitment I have sought must be made formally in the House of Commons during the course of this debate.
Dealing with the proposals that are before us, 1 would like to comment briefly on the proposals dealing with Private Members' Business. For many years, private Members have been frustrated by the system presently in place whereby it is possible for any determined group to prevent any given private Member's proposal from ever coming to a decision. It is highly desirable that at least some degree of relief from this restriction be found, and I know that this is the intent of the Governments proposed changes to the Standing Orders regard-

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
ing Private Members' Business. However, this is not to say that the method for relieving this frustration should be contrary to the fundamentals of our system.
I am seriously concerned that the system now proposed, even with the changes that have been made since the draft Standing Orders were tabled before Christmas, still could be manipulated in such a way that it would contravene the principle that the Government of the day should and must take responsibility for the process by which important decisions on issues of major national concern are taken, and, even more importantly, the principle that all such proposals are given the fullest possible consideration at all stages before the House is asked to pronounce its final opinion. The proposal as it now stands may still, although not intentionally, threaten these fundamental requirements.
Five hours of House time at the second reading stage of many important legislative initiatives may very often be sufficient, whether the proposal is that of the Government or of a private Member. However, I think Members would agree that it would be clearly inadequate on some issues, and this is especially true regarding issues of great social importance on which decisions will be permitted td depend on the personal views of Members as opposed to Party positions, and on which quite naturally they would require more time than usual for explanations of individual courses of action.
I do recognize that the proposal would require that any item once debated would go to the bottom of the priority list thereby giving opponents and proponents alike a period of weeks if not months in which to alert the public at large as to the nature of the proposition. This, however, does not fully meet the guarantee required that issues of great national import receive the full and complete consideration of the House.
Why do I say this? While there is a maximum number of hours provided for consideration of a proposal at second reading and at the post-committee stages, there is no minimum time.
What is proposed is that 20 Private Members' Bills be selected by lot to have some priority and the committee on Private Members' Business will select six of these which will then actually come to a decision by vote after limited debate. This committee would understandably be composed of a majority of Government supporters, and it will be able not only to select the six Bills that will come to a vote but to determine how much debate they will be allowed on second reading stage up to a maximum of five hours.
The Government's proposal to ensure that there is adequate time for public input on each of these measures is based on the premise that each measure will receive five hours of debate, but this is not the case. This is not what a close reading of the revised proposals to amend the Standing Orders tabled late last week actually say. The committee can decide to give a measure, or all six of the measures no more than one hour's debate each on second reading stage. In that case, the Government's proposal to stretch out the time for consideration
through a rotation system to allow the public to become informed and state its position will not come into effect at all.
The Government's proposal, therefore, on this aspect of Private Members' Business, must be changed so that every one of the six measures which will be selected for super priority and be allowed to come to a vote get the full five hours of debate, unless there is unanimous consent by the House to do differently. In short, the five hours must be a minimum and not a maximum time for debate on second reading.
As well, there is no guarantee whatsoever in the proposed Standing Orders regarding how one of these items selected for super priority might be treated in committee, and that Government supporters will not try to ram it through in only one or two committee meetings. These problems are compounded by the element of the proposal whereby the House itself would have no opportunity to debate or alter the decision of a Private Members' Business committee with regard to which items must be brought to a vote and how long they may be debated. There is no procedure in the proposed Standing Orders covering this, and in my view it is not enough to say that the House can change anything by unanimous consent.
Let me be frank. This system, even with the changes made, leaves open the potential for abuse either through manipulation of committee work or other forms of perhaps inadvertent connivance by a Government not willing to assume its responsibility for presenting controversial measures to Parliament. For the proposal for Private Members' Business to be one for which our support could be expected, there must be at least one further change made of the kind about which I have talked. There must be no way for a Private Members' Business committee to decide that a measure selected to come to a vote will receive only one hour's debate in the crucial second reading stage.
I would like now to turn to the proposal for the report stage that, if improperly used, could render that stage redundant and could seriously impair the rights of Members to bring important issues before the whole House for determination. I am seriously concerned about the proposed "Note" to be added to Standing Order 81(10). The report stage is intended to be a final appeal to the House as a whole from a decision of a limited group of members; or, in the case of matters of procedural dispute, from decisions by persons of less experience, knowledge and sophistication than those, with all due respect, we may find in the Chair and at the Table in the House at present.
In my view the present proposal is too strongly phrased. I fear it could be interpreted in a way which would be too rigorously restrictive. If the "Note" were to be interpreted literally and rigorously applied, then our legislative process would be seriously unbalanced and would be considered to be most unfair in its operation. It would certainly be inconsistent with our system of checks and balances and the desire to enhance the role of Private Members, not to mention the role of opposition Parties, for whom presenting amendments is a
February 11, 1986

crucial way to formally state how they think the Government's legislative proposals could be improved and to force the Government to take a stand on their alternatives.
I would now like to turn to the proposals in the Government's motion with respect to standing committees. As 1 indicated earlier, I have some serious reservations concerning the over-all thrust of the recommendations of the Special Committee with regard to committee structure. I welcome the proposals which would enhance the powers of Standing Committees to initiate investigations on subjects of their own choosing.
As someone who has had the honour of serving in the House in almost every conceivable capacity, including as a private Member in Opposition, as a Private Member on the Government side, as a committee chairman dealing with one of the most important things with which a committee can deal; that is, the decennial revision of the Bank Act, as a Private Member who had once been in Cabinet and was then out while his Government was still in office, and now as House Leader of the Official Opposition-I think I have some perspective which I can honestly bring to these deliberations.
As I have said, while I welcome proposals which would enhance the powers of standing committees to initiate investigations on subjects of their own choosing, I have my personal doubts about the utility of having many small standing committees going about their diverse activities while the legislative work in their fields is parcelled off to separate ad hoc legislative committees.
I believe that if the committee system in place since 1968 were to have the enhanced terms of reference proposed by the special committee, and as set out in the Government's proposals we are discussing today, then they would have greater potential for achieving the goals which we desire. Members wishing to specialize in particular areas may do so in the type of framework I have mentioned without the risk of defusing their related activities on legislative, expenditure and policy matters, whose consideration would be divided between separate standing and legislative committees. I am concerned that the system set out in the proposal could-and I hope it will not if it is adopted-lead Members off on tangents and away from the major issues of the day. In this way they would be diverted from addressing important matters in their chosen fields of interest when they are brought before the House by the Government in the most tangible and meaningful form of parliamentary consideration-the form of legislation.
Everyone recognizes that the most effective and powerful committee system in any deliberative body in the world is that employed in the Congress of the United States. I point out that in Congress there is only a single system of large standing committees, each with a comprehensive mandate over not just investigations but Government expenditure and legislation. In the process each makes ample use of subcommittees.
As I have said, from my own experience here in a whole range of capacities I cannot help but wonder whether the proposed new system will not prove to be merely a way of diverting Members from the real issues when presented in the
Standing Orders
form of Government legislation. In the long run, unless we are very careful, it could be more frustrating than helpful.
There is no assurance from this Government that when a standing committee is holding an inquiry into a subject that the Government will wait until the inquiry is over before presenting legislation to the House and to an entirely separate legislative committee. The Government has given no assurance that when a standing committee is reviewing a Government policy or an administrative decision it will not go ahead and act in any event before the committee completes its deliberations. An example of this is the way this Government first refused any committee hearings with respect to the sale of de Havilland to Boeing and then later caved in and agreed to hold hearings. However, it said it would not take into account the evidence or conclusions of those committee hearings. It then went ahead and to all intents and purposes closed the deal to sell de Havilland to Boeing two days before the committee completed its work. That is not a very good example of how what the Government is proposing will actually work.
At this point I may as well indicate my Party's and my serious concern about the proposal to limit the kind and number of questions which any Member may have on the Order Paper at any one time. The Government has not taken up the Special Committee's quid pro quo of permitting members of committees studying Estimates to submit a fixed number of written questions in advance, nor has the Government shown any interest in improving the speed with which written questions are now answered. As a result, this new limitation on seeking information could seriously impair the rights of Members to seek information on Government activities. We hope for real assurances from the Government with respect to this matter, not merely in the form of promises but in the form of tangible evidence in the way it tables answers to questions which are now lying on the current Order Paper, in some cases for more than a year.
Also, Mr. Speaker, since you, under the current and proposed rules, can direct someone asking a question during the Oral Question Period to put it on the Order Paper, the Member of Parliament to whom this direction is made can be completely frustrated in his or her efforts, if that Member already has four questions on the Order Paper and the Government is stalling in answering them. That outlet which the rules provide will really be limited.
There are many other areas touched upon by these proposals: the timing of Routine Proceedings, the method of taking divisions, the making of Orders in the House, the provision of a registry of a Member's external travels, and many other important issues. I am sure my colleagues will be addressing all these matters, and others, during this debate.
With respect to the proposal for a registry of a Member's travels outside the country, and the payment for those travels by other Governments or non-governmental organizations, we think there is a major gap. There is no requirement to list trips paid for by the Government when the Government sends Members abroad to represent it, or includes Members on its official delegations; nor do trips taken abroad by Ministers and
10668

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
paid for out of public funds have to be included. This means that the proposal in the form presented today for a registry of a Member's external travel could largely cover travel by opposition MPs, which would give a distorted and perhaps unintentionally misleading picture, since the large amount of travel by Government MPs allegedly on behalf of the Government, or through being a part of Government delegations, would not be included.
With respect to the taking of divisions and the length of time bells can ring before a vote is taken, the Conservatives, when in opposition, argued that the ability to control how long bells ring before a vote is taken is important for an Official Opposition to get a Government too secure in its majority to at least listen-not necessarily to change its legislative proposals in question, but at least to allow more time for debate, to allow committee hearings, or to divide a complex Bill into several simpler and more clear-cut propositions in individual Bills. If the potentially unlimited ringing of bells as a possible parliamentary tactic by an Opposition is to be given up, then surely the Government has to confirm at the very least that it will not abuse its majority and prevent the adequate consideration of major legislation and major administration proposals.
I also want to say that the measure before us would give the Speaker new authority to have Members leave the House when they are what we call being "named". However, the proposal before us goes far beyond what is recommended, if I am not mistaken, in the report of the special committee. It not only says, Mr. Speaker, that you can suspend an Hon. Member from the service of the House without motion for the balance of the day, but also if this happens on a second occasion you can do so for a period of five days without any recourse or appeal to the House as a whole. I must say, Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to you, and all future incumbents of the Chair, that this goes beyond the recommendation of the Special Committee, and we certainly think it is excessive.
If these proposals, like any reforms, are to work, it will depend on a great deal of effort and good will, especially on the part of the Government. On this point, I look at this Government's track record and, contrary to what the Government House Leader has said, it is not encouraging. I have already mentioned as one example the way in which the Government handled the de Havilland case without due regard to Parliament.
There is an even more troubling indication of the Government's intentions and purposes. I refer to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in Montreal just yesterday, as reported in a Canadian press dispatch. The Prime Minister was talking about his good friend, Ronald Reagan, the President of the United States, when he said, and I quote: "He doesn't have to face the House of Commons every day. It's an almost ideal situation". Let me repeat that. The Prime Minister, who should be the first among Parliamentarians, said in Montreal last night when speaking of Ronald Reagan: "He
doesn't have to face the House of Commons every day. It's an almost ideal situation".
Shame!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If this is what the Prime Minister, who is and should be the first among Parliamentarians, thinks about Parliament, how can we have any real confidence in the Government's intentions with respect to these reform proposals and the way in which the Government would operate if this, or any other package of reform, were to be adopted? If the Prime Minister is going to ignore the Canadian people by ignoring their elected representatives in Parliament, and if he is secretly hankering for the U.S. presidential system, let him be more forthright. Let his Government propose changes in Parliament which will establish not just those changes he wants but all of the checks and balances of the presidential and congressional system.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, what happened to the supposed interest of the Government in lessening the necessity for the confidence of the House to be at stake every time the Government presents a proposal? That is not in these proposals anywhere at all and was not, as far as I recall, anywhere in the speech of the Government House Leader. Let us be frank, if the private Members' role is to be enhanced, one of the prerequisites is that the Government make a formal commitment that it is going to have much less recourse in insisting that the confidence of the House and, therefore, the future of the Government is at stake when Government measures are proposed. That is not a problem in the American system which is liked so well by the Prime Minister. After all, those members stay for a fixed period of time no matter what happens to the Government's legislation. But we have nothing from the Government House Leader on this matter.
In our House of Commons, the Opposition Parties as well as individual private Members have to be able to check and hold to account the executive in order that its actions be properly scrutinized, in order to be able to alter Government legislation and in order to present and have considered meaningful alternatives. The Prime Minister cannot surreptitiously or openly try to weaken the existing parliamentary system on the one hand and, on the other hand, have his House Leader talk about strengthening the role of private Members and of Parliament itself.
The Government House Leader talked earlier this morning about how his Government wants to make Parliament once again the centre of the real consideration of the great issues of the day. But this is not what the Prime Minister said yesterday in Montreal. He said just the opposite. And who speaks for the Government? In our parliamentary system it is still the case that first and foremost it is the Prime Minister and he has just, in effect, cancelled out the well intended, I trust, words of the Government House Leader.
The first step to real parliamentary reform is for the Prime Minister and his Ministers to commit to be in Parliament regularly and frequently to answer to the House, and they have a lot to answer for already.
February 11, 1986

The Official Opposition and I favour parliamentary reform, real reform, but we received the latest version of the Government's package only late last week and a more detailed study of these proposals has raised new and serious questions in our minds. These questions have been enhanced in concern and intensity by the intemperate and troubling words of the Prime Minister last night. We believe in parliamentary reform but these new questions have been raised and we have not yet received the answers.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) on his excellent speech. I would like to refer him to the "Note" which appears on page 1666 wherein you, Mr. Speaker, seem to be put in an extremely difficult position when it comes to the report stage of a Bill. The Speaker is expected to judge and determine motions which are of exceptional significance and to determine whether or not they would warrant further consideration at that report stage. Would the Hon. Member for Windsor West care to comment as to the difficulty the Speaker would encounter in making such a political decision?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very concept of a committee is that it is a smaller body to which a question is referred by a larger body. The committee is subordinate to the larger body. The proposal of the Government turns that on its head, because it states that normally the House as a whole will not be able to overturn decisions of what is supposed to be its subordinate body on matters of procedure, and normally will not be able to deal with questions which came before the committee in the form of amendments. As I have said, I believe this turns the basic concept of what a committee is on its head.
It might be argued that there is an escape clause for the Speaker to avoid the problems mentioned by the Hon. Member because the direction to the Speaker has the word "normally" included in it. But what does "normally" mean? It means that the usual, customary, every-day practice is to do what is in the instructions. Therefore, every time a report stage comes forward, there is a risk that the incumbent of the Chair, the Speaker, will have to make a decision-which can well be attacked as being political-to not allow an amendment ruled out of order in the committee to be argued and considered again on its acceptability from the point of view of the rules in the full House, nor in allowing the House as a whole to take a look at an amendment which was presented in the committee.
The Speaker already has the authority, which he uses, to group amendments, and this has saved a lot of time on report stage. It seems to me that we have to give serious consideration as to whether the need is simply a more active use of the authority the Speaker already has to group amendments, rather than putting the Speaker into what could be an untenable position of making decisions which will inevitably run the risk of being considered political because they deal with the merits of amendments as well as their acceptability under the rules rather than some mechanical grouping or organization of the debate.
Standing Orders
I think there is peril in this amendment for the rights of the individual Member of Parliament and for Members organized in Parties to have their views considered formally in the form of amendments. Perhaps, in the long run, there is an even more serious threat to the position of the Chair and the appearance and reality it must have of complete impartiality.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one or two quick comments and then ask the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) a question. The remarks of the Hon. Member reminded me of the words of the philosopher: "All is yellow to the jaundiced eye". This reform package may not be perfect, but it is so much better than anything we have had before that every Hon. Member should be dancing with joy. We are not saying it is perfect, but it is certainly a tremendous move forward.
With reference to questions on the Order Paper, l would like to remind the Hon. Member for Windsor West that I had a question on the Order Paper from 1980 until 1985 and never got an answer. At least we are moving ahead with the answers to questions on the Order Paper. My question was not too difficult. All I wanted to know was how many defeated Liberal candidates had been invited to the dinner for President Reagan. It was a very simple question, but I could not get answer in four and a half years.
The last point I would like to make has regard to Private Members' Bills. The proposed reforms represent a tremendous advance in this area. I look forward to the day when we will no longer be talking out important Bills. The Hon. Member mentioned that we should have a minimum period of debate. I would like him to enlarge on that. If no one wants to discuss a Bill, why require a minimum time for debate? If Members do want to discuss it, they can continue for the maximum time, but to impose a minimum time would be defeating the whole purpose. People would be talking simply for the sake of talking. Would the Hon. Member enlarge on what he meant when he said that there should be a minimum time for debate on Private Members', Bills?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who just spoke showed why it was important for me to make the comments which I made previously. He himself has raised what could be a problem, which we on the Opposition side have identified, with respect to the proposal regarding Private Members' Business. Under the Government's proposal the Private Members' Business committee can select six measures of the 20 that are selected by lot, which will be decided upon through a vote. A majority of Members on that committee can say that one of those six measures need only have one hour of debate, or may have a maximum of five hours.
The Hon. Member's House Leader has recognized the concern of opposition Members that the proposal for bringing Private Members' Business to a vote could be used to slip through the House, without adequate debate, a major matter which, first, should be one for which the Government at least takes the responsibility of bringing before the House and.

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
second, there is assurance that it has at least as much debate as a minor Bill normally has under our rules when presented by the Government.
The way this is written, if the majority of the members of that Private Members' Business committee agree, the protection which the Government itself said is necessary to prevent something from slipping through the House without adequate debate of at least five hours, those five hours being strung out over a series of weeks, will not take place. If the Private Members' Business committee formed by a majority, in this case, of Government Members, say that a measure needs only one hour of debate, the protection which his own Government House Leader says is necessary will not come into play. The very first time debate on second reading on one of these six measures comes up in the House there will have to be a vote after one hour, if that is what the committee has decided. There will not be rotation with the other measures which require debate before coming to a vote.
1 urge my hon. friend to look at the real concern which I have expressed, not simply because I have expressed it, but because his own House Leader has agreed with what I have said. I, in a constructive way, have been trying to point out a way to help the Government better achieve what it feels is necessary to achieve.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) a question about the proposal with respect to the power of the Speaker to name Members of this House. The Member for Windsor West indicated in his comments that he believed the proposal was excessive. I agree with the Member and I have some very serious concerns about the proposal which, as I understand, was not a proposal by the committee, but was a government proposal.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, there is no greater right of a Member of Parliament than to sit here in the House of Commons. That right is the result of being elected by one's constituents in a general election. That is the greatest right, and 1 believe that that right should be taken away in only very extraordinary circumstances. Who should have the right to remove a Member from the House? Ultimately, the electors in any particular constituency should have the right to remove a Member from the House. In my view, only the House should have the ultimate right to remove a Member between elections.
With all due respect, Sir, this proposal gives you ultimate authority to decide whether a Member should continue to sit in the House. I do not think that is right. Given the fact that it is on ultimate right, only one's peers in the House should be given the authority to remove one from the House. Under the present system the Speaker can name a particular Member and, on motion, that Member can be removed from the House or suspended for the day. One's peers have to make that decision. The Government is proposing that the Speaker be given the authority to name a Member without resort to motion, not only for one sitting day, but for up to five days on a second naming.
Will the Member for Windsor West expand upon his comments with respect to his position that this proposal is excessive? Does the Member agree with me that the ultimate authority to suspend a Member from the House should rest with other Members in the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are arguments on both sides. As a practical matter, the suspension by the Speaker of a Member for the balance of a sitting for alleged misconduct in the House is almost automatic now. The custom is-and I have never seen it happen differently-that when a Speaker names a Member the Government House Leader automatically moves a motion to support the Speaker and all the Government Members vote with him. As a practical matter, a proposal limited to the right of a Speaker to have someone suspended from the House for the balance of a day's sitting does not really change what is happening now. However, it will prevent the naming of a Member and the vote on that naming from blanking out a Question Period, if the incident takes place during Question Period. I think we would agree that for all Members, especially Members in Opposition, the ability to question the Government is something very important and precious.
Finally, I repeat what I said in my speech, that I do not believe there are grounds for giving the Speaker, the incumbent of the Chair, the right to suspend a Member for five days during a sitting on being named a second time. I believe that is excessive, although I can see arguments pro and con for the Speaker being able to name someone on his own accord for the balance of a day. I believe the Speaker in the United Kingdom House of Commons can do that at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments have now terminated.

Mr. Speaker, this could be a great day for Parliament. I say that it could be because there are a number of conditions attached to that hopeful prediction. My hope arises from the work I have been involved in since being appointed to the Lefebvre Committee on Parliamentary Reform and subsequently the Special Committee on Reform of the House chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
In order for this to be a significant day, we must continue the spirit of flexibility, accommodation, compromise and nonpartisan debate that accompanied this process since its beginning and should these reforms be adopted, Members of Parliament, both individually and collectively, whether in committee or in the House, will have to actively use these new powers to create a new Parliament. They will, as the popular expression has it, have to "go for it".
May I also suggest that what we have here is only half the package of parliamentary reform. The Government House Leader has acknowledged that we are dealing with the procedural half of parliamentary reform and that there are still nearly 30 recommendations of the committee with which to
February 11, 1986

deal. Outstanding reforms include administrative reform of the House, the organization of Parliament Hill itself, the recommendations concerning broadcasting of the House of Commons and sound availability in committees. That was a recommendation in our second report which has yet to proceed. Other recommendations include the expansion of the CBC parliamentary channel into a Canadian equivalent of C-SPAN. I suggest the adoption of these recommendations would go a long way to better informing the public about Parliament. I understand that on Friday the Government House Leader made a commitment to proceed with these recommendations.
Although this motion is a Government proposal, we are dealing with a procedural package which is very close to what the committee recommended. In some ways it is unfortunate that we must deal with this motion as a Government proposal because it may provoke a somewhat partisan debate. However, even members of the committee had second thoughts and wanted the Government to change some recommendations so that dealing with this motion as a Government proposal was unavoidable. Otherwise, it would have been necessary to adopt the committee's procedural recommendations without incorporating any of the changes recommended by committee members and other Members of the House.
It is unfortunate that the Government did not rely enough on experts who were close to the work of the committee in preparing its procedural package. The Government could perhaps have saved itself some problems in attempting to devise the Standing Orders. In that respect, I think the process could have been better. Furthermore, it is important to note that this motion is the result of consultation rather than negotiation.
The Government has demonstrated some flexibility because it has dealt with many of the criticisms we raised last fall. My greatest criticism concerned parliamentary secretaries sitting on Standing Committees. The proposed Standing Orders strictly prohibit this from taking place. In addition, I am grateful that the Government House Leader has dropped his proposal to have the Government define "confidence", in the myriad and convoluted ways once contemplated by the Government House Leader. Thank God for that.
The Government has also demonstrated a welcome flexibility in meeting the objection raised by my colleagues about the description of Private Members' Business as it appeared in the proposed Standing Orders just before Christmas. If those Standing Orders had been adopted at that time it would have been possible for the five hours that might be allocated to a votable item to be allocated consecutively by the Special Committee on Private Members' Business. I understand that this would not be possible under the present Standing Orders and that a Bill which was allocated five hours would be debated one hour at a time with a full nineteen hours of Private Members' Business in between those hours. If I understand correctly, if Private Members' Business could not be dealt with we would revert to Government business. This reflects a concern of my caucus that there be appropriate "political time" for Private Members' Business.
Standing Orders
The committee was also cognizant of the fact that if private Members were to be given the new responsibility of being able to cause a Bill to come to a division and, if passed, become law, the process should have some of the same safeguards accorded to Government legislation. This safeguard gives the public enough time to mobilize and react to certain legislation. Such a requirement to prevent Private Members' Bills from being quickly passed applies to all legislation that comes to the House. Private Members' Business is not being singled out. I am pleased that the Government has moved in that respect.
The Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) made a good technical point, that the possibility still exists that the committee on Private Members' Business could make a bad decision and allot only one hour for a matter that deserves five hours of deliberation. This is something the Government might consider because, without sounding naive, the consideration for the allotment of time for many of these questions depends to a great extent on respect on the part of the chairman and members of that committee for what should be debated for the maximum amount of time. Our committee operated in a co-operative and trusting environment and tended to make recommendations with such an atmosphere in mind. We know that such an environment will not always exist, and I suggest the Government consider the point made by the Hon. Member for Windsor West.
I remind the House that the Private Members' Business Committee is intended to be appointed by the Speaker rather than the Government, and that the chairman of the committee will be someone who is selected from the panel of committee chairmen. In many respects then this committee is not an arm of the Government, although it will consist of a majority of government Members. The concerns of the Member for Windsor West and the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) warrant consideration, but the success of this proposal ultimately depends on whether we live up to the spirit of the reform or simply maintain the same old attitude.
In this respect I say to Government Members, whether they be cabinet members or backbenchers, that a lot-the future, the vitality and the integrity of Parliament-will depend on the extent to which you allow this reform to work in keeping with the spirit of the reform itself, not letting short-term political considerations get in the way of what could be a very, very exciting new era for the Canadian Parliament. Much depends, as I say, on the attitude the Government takes to these reforms.
I would like to add some caveats about what has been recommended by the Government; concern, for instance, is in order about the Standing Orders having to do with report stage amendments. I am not so concerned about the ability of the Speaker to rule out amendments that have already been considered in committee. That is something the committee recommended, and I stand by that recommendation. In that sense, as I understand it, we are only going back to a system that was in place some time ago.

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
I think though that the Speaker ought to have a little more flexibility than is given to him by the proposed Standing Orders. The Speaker should be able to look at an amendment that was considered out of order in committee which in the Speaker's judgment was a bad ruling, because there is such a thing as human imperfection. The Speaker should, in my view, have the flexibility to say that, notwithstanding what happened in the committee, something might be brought forward again, even though ruled out of order in committee. I ask the Government to consider that suggestion.
When I ask the Government to consider these things I am not necessarily asking it to consider them in the context of amending the proposal that we have before us today, but to consider these changes on the assumption that they are going to say or do what the Hon. Member for Windsor West asked, i.e. give a commitment that as we move along, even within the experimental period, there be an ability and a willingness to change things and to say: "Yes, we should have covered that, but we did not. Let us change it." I think that is the kind of spirit we need as we enter into this experimental period.
I see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is here now. Let me say that I hope the Government will, as we enter into this experimental period, be open to things we discover as we go along. It does not matter how much effort you give to the drafting of these Standing Orders, there is always an odd wrinkle here and there that no one ever thought of, and I think it is very important the Government move with that attitude in mind.
Some of the ways in which the Government's proposal is different from what the committee recommended also need to be put on the record. For instance, substitution on committees. The committee recommended that members be made permanent members of the smaller standing commitees and they, and they alone, have the ability to designate their substitute. That had to do with the notion of building up a sense of tenure on a committee.
The Government has recommended that people who are appointed to these committees be able to name a group of five from which they could draw for substitution. This group of five has to be signified by the whip of the Party in question, depending on which Member is affected. We have two problems. One, we still have the whips involved and that could erode the independence of the member on the committee. Second, we also have the problem of what do independents do. We have an independent Member in this Parliament, at least so called. What does an independent Member do in terms of getting a list of five people to substitute for him on committee? That is just one of a few problems that I wanted to put on the record.
With respect to questions, Mr. Speaker, and this is very important, here is where you clearly run into the dangers of tampering with the package the reform committee put together. On the face of it, limiting Members to four questions on the Order Paper at any given time looks like a very severe restriction of Members' ability to ask questions. I say, I think fairly, that it is more of a restriction on Members who were in
the habit of using the Order Paper for questions. It is not something of which I have done a lot so I probably will not feel it as much as other people who have been very successful at using this route for calling attention to issues, but the committee agreed to that, Mr. Speaker, because there was a trade off. We agreed because at the same time in our package we allowed for Members to submit 10 written questions on the Estimates on whatever committee they happened to be working. It was the trade-off, a quid pro quo or whatever it is called. I think the Government has made a mistake in tampering with that recommendation. It made the package more unacceptable to people who were looking to find things wrong with it by giving them a kind of legitimate thing on which to hang their hat. I do not know why we could not have gone ahead with the 10 written questions proposal.
I am glad to see some of the cleaning up that has been done on previous proposals that were adopted. Some of the problems came, admittedly, because the Government adopted the committee's recommendations holus-bolus, particularly the problems that came with legislative committees. The committee had recommended that legislative committees be made up of 20 members. The Government adopted the committee's report and so we got legislative committees made up of 20 members.
We have now in these new Standing Orders, if they are adopted, more flexibility. We could have larger legislative committees. I hope we do not, Mr. Speaker. I hope that a 30 member committee will be used only for constitutional amendments or something like that. I hope we will see smaller legislative committees. I also hope that whoever speaks for the Government next will say why there appears to be no attempt to establish some sort of traffic control with respect to legislative committees.
Does the Government have some process in mind which could be reached between the Parties outside of the Standing Orders for limiting the number of legislative committees, or is this just an oversight? I hope the next person who speaks for the Government will indicate what the Government intends to do about a problem that I believe was raised by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) having to do with the proliferation of legislative committees.
Finally, some advice to the Government on today's proceedings. If these proposals are adopted, if the spirit of these proposals is lived up to and if in the coming weeks and months the appropriate changes are made when we discover things that were not apparent to us when we passed the Standing Orders, we will be entering into a whole new area of parliamentary politics, a whole new parliamentary process.
I think the Government should consider that it is all right for the House to take the time it needs to have everything said that Members feel should be said before this proposal comes to a vote or to an agreement, whatever the case may be. I hope that is something we could do unanimously or at least by consensus. I think it is very important that it not only be seen to be done that way but that it genuinely be that. For that reason I encourage the Government to listen carefully to the various reservations that, Members have about the proposal
February 11, 1986

before them. I hope the Government will do what it can immediately in terms of actual changes, or commitments that it will be possible for changes to be made. The Government should do what it can about that today.
I also encourage Hon. Members on my right, in the Liberal Party, to see their way through some of the understandable reservations which come from their day-to-day dealings with the Government and to seek a higher ground. 1 encourage them to try to see this process through to completion. As one who has been involved with it-it seems since time immemorial-I hope we can bring at least one important stage of parliamentary reforms, and there are others to go, to completion today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to enter the debate very briefly. I realize 1 only have a few moments, and I will not take many more than that. I should begin by complimenting the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) for the tremendous role which he played in this major initiative in parliamentary reform. I pay tribute as well to all members of the committee, to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who played a very significant role in developing what is an historic intervention on behalf of parliamentarians with regard to the evolution and reform of our institution, the House of Commons, and, of course, to the very distinguished Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who has led, with great leadership and sensitivity, Members of the House of Commons to unanimous recommendations with regard to the reform of this fundamental institution. I salute his leadership and the great distinction which he brings to himself and to the House with this report on reform of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Hon. Members will recall that in the Speech from the Throne the Government outlined its intentions to embarks upon a process of parliamentary reform in the following words:
First, you must critically examine the relationship of Parliament with the people of Canada. Members of the House of Commons will be asked to approve the appointment of a parliamentary task force on reform ... The central focus of this task force will be the enhancement of the role of the private member. From that perspective the task force will examine and make recommendations concerning the powers, practices, organization and resources of the Commons.
I would remind the House as well that in September, 1985,1 announced a broad package of reform initiatives, including a review of Order in Council appointments by a standing commute of the House. Last fall, again, the Government announced a register of interests by Members of Parliament and a proposal for a register of lobbyists. Let me point out that the amendments before the House represent a consensus reached after consultation with representatives of the Opposition Parties.
Standing Orders

Those, Mr. Speaker, were the specific recommendations formulated by the Committee. I admit that 1 was impressed by the role of a Member of Parliament when I came here for the first time in September 1983, which makes me a very junior Member compared with a Member who has now been sitting in the House for twenty-eight years, and 1 am referring to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and there are many more. I was greatly influenced by some of my reactions and observations, and that is why 1 decided to take action shortly after I was sworn in as Prime Minister. Let me explain:

One of the first things which struck me as I entered the House of Commons for the first time, as Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, was the fact that this represented democracy, these were the leaders of communities across Canada and yet, in point of fact, the Member of Parliament had less influence in the decision-making process in this town than an Assistant Deputy Minister of any given Department. The erosion of influence and authority which has taken place over the years, as the bureaucracy usurped the executive functions in the decision-making process of the Member of Parliament, was something that had to be arrested and turned around so that once and for all there was a reaffirmation of the principle, dulled over the years, that this House, even with its imperfections, stands tribute to the nobility of the parliamentary system and is the authority of the elected Member of Parliament over the executive at all times and in all circumstances.
Hear, hear!

I make no pretence as a relatively new Member of Parliament to great understandings of some of the arcane rules which have governed our conduct over the years. I know that people watching us from time to time have difficulty understanding why certain things take place, as do I. I know that most people would agree, for example, that the way Question Period has evolved, and television in the House, have both served to distort and detract from the tremendous contributions in committee made by the backbench Members of Parliament, the contributions which they make to enriching the parliamentary process. However, that is life, and that is the way it has evolved and nothing will change it.
This will throw more light on the parliamentary process. It will enhance and strengthen our democracy, as do initiatives such as that brought forward by the Hon. Member who preceded me. The basis of parliamentary reform-all we are trying to do, and no one says that it is perfect-is to respond in some ways to the present situation.
[ Translation]
-the heartfelt concerns, because they were indeed heartfelt, the concerns 1 read as formulated by my hon. friend from Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), who, 1 am sure, was speaking for many Members of this House. I found a passage

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
quoted in the very beginning of the McGrath Report on Parliamentary Reform, and it was quoted from something Mr. Blaikie had said:

I think one of the reasons why a lot of people run for Parliament is that they feel they have something to say. I always thought that if I could just get to say these things in the House of Commons, that would be significant, it would matter... However, since I have come to Ottawa, everything I say is suspect, if it is listened to at all. So there is this incredible frustration. What ought to be the pinnacle of exchange of ideas is in fact the black hole in which nobody listens to anybody.
I could not have said it better myself.
Hear, hear!

I think that comment points out the frustration, and it is a comment tinged with realism. What the Hon. Member was saying to the committee and to all Members of the House of Commons was: "Help me and my colleagues elevate parliamentary debate; help us make once again the Parliament of Canada that instrument of magnificence it once was and can become again, if the role of the Member of Parliament is enhanced". Somebody once said in the House of Commons that Members of Parliament are nobodies when they get outside the House. I say that Members of Parliament are somebodies inside this House and outside this House at all times.
Hear, hear!

I want to say to my hon. friend that that was not a partisan comment. I can understand. If the term was used, I did not construe it as pejorative because in point of fact the erosion which has taken place over the decades and over the years with regard to the attributions, the responsibilities, the influence and the power of the Member of Parliament, has served to diminish the Member and, in so doing, has served to weaken the House of Commons, and when the House of Commons is weakened, democracy suffers.
What we have tried to do, imperfectly no doubt, is to reach out to the best instincts of Members of the House and say as a new Government, as we did: We can do better. We can arrest the decline of the House of Commons and we can elevate debate. We can make the role of Members more meaningful. We can make certain that Members participate in a substantial way in the decision-making process. We can make sure that when a Member of Parliament from Winnipeg, the North Shore, Cape Breton or Vancouver Island comes to Ottawa, he or she comes to Ottawa to set great questions of national policy, not to respond to the whims of bureaucrats. That is what happened and that is what now must be reversed.
Hear, hear!

I think, as I look at it, Your Honour, we have let the symbol of democracy slip. We now have an opportunity to accept this tremendous document of reform, brought about by the Hon. Member for St. John's East, the Hon. Member for Papineau and their colleagues from the
NDP. I say to you, Sir, that though imperfect, this is a splendid document, the acceptance of which will bring honour to the House of Commons, will bring honour to each and every Member.

But above all, it will bring honour to our Canadian democratic system and to all those who are a part of that system.

It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock.
