subsubtopic: SOVIET UNION-RELEASE OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is a day of triumph for human rights activists. Today is the day that gives hope to all who work from depth of heart and genuine concern on issues of man's humanity towards his fellow man. Today is a lesson learned about respect for conviction, personal strength of courage, and ability to cope with intolerance when one's firm belief in the right to practise one's religion freely and the right to rejoin one's family, wherever they may live, is not respected.
Today is a day of celebration as we witness an end to injustice with the release from Russian internment of Anatoly Shcharansky. We rejoice as he crossed to freedom rejoining his wife Avital.
Today we are witness to an act of faith, of hope, and of tenacity by thousands of people throughout the world who took heart with the signing of the Helsinki Accord, but lost hope as the Soviets disregarded their responsibility and obligations as co-signators.
As an early activist and organizer of public demonstrations in the interest of Soviet Jewry, as a member of the Interfaith Task Force of the Canadian Jewish Congress, I take this opportunity to thank the Parliament of Canada, its senior Ministers, and individual Members of Parliament who have brought the issue of Anatoly and of Soviet Jewry to the attention of Soviet ambassadors, leaders at the United Nations, as well as in the Soviet Union.
Today Canadians may take pride in knowing that their efforts have sensitized the Soviets to the importance of the
February 11, 1986

issue of human rights and the emigration of Soviet Jews in the eyes of the western world, as well as leading to the release of Anatoly Shcharansky.

subtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY TASK FORCE ON TAX SYSTEM
NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY TASK FORCE ON TAX SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you know, the New Democratic Party has been asking Canadians to make their views known on our tax system through the Tax Probe 86 Task Force chaired by the Hon. Member for Kam-loops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). What they have found so far is an existing tax system that rewards the rich and punishes middle and low-income earners. For example, advertisements appearing in the Financial Post, the Financial Times and The Globe and Mail, inserted by companies such as Wood Gundy, tell wealthy Canadians that they are able to arrange their tax reports so that they will pay no income tax on an income of $42,000 through the use of the dividend tax credit and other deductions. They can own a cruiser with 100 per cent borrowed funds generating $165,000 in tax deductions over four years. They can invest $12,500 in a hotel and receive a 60 per cent tax write-off in one year and the balance in the next.
The Task Force also knows that the average Canadian family is paying $1,000 a year more from the tax changes in the last Conservative Budget, and that single unemployed Canadians will be paying federal income tax on as little as $7,000 received in unemployment insurance benefits, that is presuming that they still qualify to receive UI. No wonder ordinary Canadians are telling Tax Probe 86 that they want a tax system that is simpler, fairer, and more efficient. That is exactly what this NDP task force will be recommending to Parliament in the months ahead.

subtopic: THIRTY-FOURTH ANNIVERSARY OF HER MAJESTY'S ACCESSION TO THE THRONE
THIRTY-FOURTH ANNIVERSARY OF HER MAJESTY'S ACCESSION TO THE THRONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this year is the thirty-fourth anniversary of Queen Elizabeth's accession to the Throne and means her reign in Canada has been the longest in Confederation. In a time when monarchists are becoming fewer, her hold on the affection of Canadians has become more secure. When we patriated our Constitution a few years ago, there was no challenge to continuing the monarchy in Canada. One reason for this was the Queen herself. During these 34 years she has been a model of service to country and devotion to family. She has exemplified the virtues of toleration and adaptability that have made Canada an island of stability in a world of turbulence.
Where other rulers must flee in the night, she remains welcome to our shores. From coast to coast Canadians know
this is a better country because we still say "God save the Queen!"

subtopic: THIRTY-FOURTH ANNIVERSARY OF HER MAJESTY'S ACCESSION TO THE THRONE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Almost daily Canadians read newspaper stories about criminals who have been released on parole and repeat violent offences similar to those which they committed previously. We heard the other day of a Scarborough man, on parole after serving 26 months of a 7-year sentence for manslaughter, violently raping a former girlfriend. On the same day we heard of a 19-year-old drifter on probation for sexual offences who attacked and raped a woman beside her three-year-old son. Such sexual offences are violent, despicable acts of human barbarism. In many countries, such acts carry the death penalty.
In Canada today many criminals are being released with little evidence of true reform, and mandatory supervision and parole regulations often allow criminals to get back to the streets where they are a threat to our society.
This Parliament should deal effectively with this issue. We have a moral obligation to initiate effective and compassionate programs for victims not only of rape but of many other serious offences which leave permanent scars on the victims. In many cases Canada's criminal justice system forgets about the suffering of victims. If we believe in justice, fairness, and the law, we owe our society not just prevention but compassion for those who suffer from the acts of barbaric human beings.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to congratulate and offer my best wishes to Anatoly Shcharansky who was today released from the Soviet Union. Anatoly Shcharansky is a leader of Soviet Jews whose role in that country of monitoring the Helsinki Final Accord brought him into direct conflict with the Government and led to his imprisonment.
The courage and bravery of this one individual who endured the pressures of the entire Soviet system to change the principles for which he stood, are a symbol not only for Jews around the world but for people everywhere who believe that basic human rights cannot be trampled. His is a triumph of the human spirit.
I wish also to pay tribute to his wife, Avital Shcharansky, who has for the past eight years travelled around the world so

February 11, 1986
many times to meet with world leaders and with concerned people everywhere, on behalf of her husband and Soviet Jews. Her travels also brought her to Canada where she and her husband have thousands of friends and supporters. Her long journey on behalf of her husband is now over, and I think we all wish her and her husband a period of peace and rest.
However, the long journey for Soviet Jews who have been denied basic rights of movement, of association and of religious freedom, is not over.
[ Translation]
There are still thousands of Jews in the Soviet Union. I think the Government of Canada and governments throughout the world should continue to pressure the Soviet authorities, so that Jews living in that country are treated fairly, as human beings, which includes having the right to emigrate if they so desire.

We do not know yet if Mr. Shcharansky's release marks a change in Soviet policy toward dissidents, but today we can hope and give thanks that one man's agony is at last over.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to say something about today's important news concerning the release of Anatoly Shcharansky. The release of Mr. Shcharansky today took place in the context of an exchange of spies between the Soviet Union and the United States and he was inappropriately included in this category.
It is of course true that the only offence Mr. Shcharansky ever committed in his life was his insistence in the Soviet Union that the Accord reached at Helsinki be observed. Mr. Shcharansky is anything but a spy. He has set an example for the world of what it means to be a courageous human being in pursuit of human liberties.
We in the Canadian House of Commons note Mr. Shcharansky's release with a great deal of pleasure. Many of us remember meeting his wife some years ago here in Ottawa when she visited our country as a part of her international attempt to obtain the release of her husband.
I conclude by simply observing that the release of Mr. Shcharansky is an important landmark for human liberty in the Soviet Union. We want to underline, however, that there remain thousands of other citizens in the Soviet Union who would like to have the same liberty. The Canadian Government, and indeed myself, on behalf of Canadians have in the past year presented a list to the Soviet Union of other citizens we would like to see obtain freedom.
Order, please. The Hon. Member's 90 seconds have expired.

subtopic: THREE-YEAR SENTENCE FOR BOY CONVICTED OF THREE MURDERS
THREE-YEAR SENTENCE FOR BOY CONVICTED OF THREE MURDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians were outraged and horrified to learn that a 15-year-old boy in Scarborough will receive three years' punishment for killing three people. The three-year sentence for three murders is, I believe, a travesty of justice. Yet under the Young Offenders Act that is the maximum allowable sentence.
What kind of signal does a case like this send to young people across Canada? Does it tell them that killing is wrong and that criminals are severely punished for crimes they commit? What do we as lawmakers say to the victims of crime who suffer the traumatic consequences of criminal activity? What do we say to the relatives of the seven-year old girl this boy brutally killed?
The Defence Council in this case was quoted as saying: "As a human being, I have difficulty with the sentence. Three years for three murders is hard to accept". Indeed it is.
I applaud the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty) for the commitment he has made to reform the sentencing provisions in the Young Offenders Act and I urge him to pursue those reforms as quickly and expeditiously as possible. Canadians can wait no longer.

Mr. Speaker, parliamentary reform is certainly a noble concept to contemplate. It is one to which everyone rather readily gives all of the appropriate lip service. However, I have noticed that there was always a certain degree of surprise and even amazement when ideas for parliamentary reform have to be put into practice or implemented because it turns out that this means change. Today, it means changing some of our Standing Orders, the rules by which we conduct ourselves in this place from day to day.
One can certainly speak of parliamentary reform in most eloquent and, perhaps, poetic terms, but when it comes to changing the Standing Orders it is rather more prosaic, mundane and down-to-earth. It is surprising how quickly enthusiasm for parliamentary reform can be replaced by a certain measure of reluctance to proceed.
That reminds me of something which was said of a certain leader of the day. It was said of him that he loved people; it was individuals he could not stand. We love parliamentary reform, but we seem to have trouble with our Standing Orders and changing them. I want to say to the House that we badly need some changes.
The Canadian people certainly are not overly impressed by the way in which we conduct ourselves in this place and how we conduct what they consider to be the important business of our nation. Now that we have television they have witnessed or heard about some rather strange happenings in this place. For example, they have seen the storming of the Chair. There have been long bell-ringing incidents and questions on the Order Paper, inquiries from Hon. Members, which are not answered for years. There are petitions which are read, petitions containing the signatures of our constituents with respect to matters of concern, grievances. The constituents ask: "Whatever happened to that petition? What became of it?" We have no answer to that question expect to say that it went missing in action.
Limbo.

That's right, limbo.
Then there are the Members of Parliament who do not occupy the front benches of the Government or Opposition and who often appear to the Canadian people to be mere spectators to all which is taking place, either cheering or jeering as the case may be.
It is certainly exhilarating to talk about reform. It is a kind of mountain-top experience, but we now have to get down into the valley of reality. We have to try to revise some of our Standing Orders. When we do that, the approach suddenly becomes not so high sounding. Rather, there is a good deal of suspicion and uncertainty. Questions are asked such as, what is in these rule changes which will aid the Opposition in doing
Standing Orders
what it is supposed to do? What is there in these rules which will further strengthen the hand of Government? Are there some hidden snares which we have missed and which are designed to trap political Parties, especially those in opposition?
Have you ever noticed, Mr. Speaker, that there seems to be a failure to ask other important questions such as, what is best for Parliament? How can we restore to this institution the type of respect and dignity which I believe it deserves? That was the approach taken by the committee headed by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who has been given praise for the outstanding work he has done for this House. When the members of the committee did their work they were not trying to pit opposition Parties against the governing Party but to do something for Parliament and something for the Members of Parliament. They wanted to find out how we can better enable Members of Parliament to serve their constituents and to work for the national good.
There is a danger in this House for members of political Parties to become too self-serving. I do not think there is anyone who will speak in this debate who is seriously seeking to destroy or undermine the partisan nature of this place. That is too silly to even contemplate. We know that the Government was elected to govern, and it had its supporters. It was elected to propose policies and programs of legislation to Parliament. The Opposition is here to ensure that the Government is accountable and to attempt to change the Government's course of direction when opposition Members or Parties consider that course of direction to be undesirable or disastrous. In that there is bound to be a clash. It is sometimes noisy and emotional. Sometimes it is not all that pleasant to observe. However, I tell Hon. Members that it is a lot better than fighting in the streets. We know that there can be excesses. There can be excesses in our partisanship. Therefore, our rules are designed to strike a fair and appropriate balance between the Government and the Opposition and among all political Parties.
In all of this there is one important aspect which may be forgotten, that is, the Member of Parliament. They want to exercise at least some degree of influence over public policy. They want to and are able to innovate and initiate. Those persons who are elected to this place need some room to live, more and have their being. That is what the McGrath Committee report was trying to achieve. Of course, nothing would help more than if we had some major attitudinal changes. However, leaving that aside, it cannot be brought about by any rule changes. Therefore, we must get on and do the best we can with our Standing Orders.
The Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), who was the representative from our Party on the McGrath Committee, and I have considered carefully and seriously the entire package of changes to the Standing Orders. We have looked at them with care. The Hon. Member for Papineau will speak for himself on the specifics, but our general view is that there are more pluses than minuses in these proposed changes. It is our

view that this is a positive approach and a positive response to parliamentary reform.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope that is both the good news and the bad news.

I suppose the Government House Leader wonders whether the bad news is yet to come. Of course we will suggest some modest changes. However, over-all we think that it is a good package of revisions contained in the proposals which have come from the Government.
For example, I ask Hon. Members to consider Standing Order 1, with which probably few Members and many Canadian people are not aware. Up until now, in seeking precedents for our procedures we have been limited, or restricted, to those practices which have been established in the Parliament of the United Kingdom. This revision to Standing Order 1 will allow us to draw upon experience elsewhere- elsewhere in Canada and elsewhere in the Commonwealth where parliamentary institutions are alive and well and flourishing but are somewhat different. That is a positive change. It will help us all a great deal as we evolve. Parliaments must evolve. They cannot just stay the way they are. They have to undergo continuous change.
I would now like to speak about the issue of the bells. I am delighted to say that if we adopt the changes to the Standing Orders, as I am convinced we will, we will then solve the problem of the long bells. The long bells are of rather recent history in the Parliament of Canada and I think that problem came about as a result of many factors. Some day some one will write the history of the long bells, I suppose, but I believe there was excessive partisanship involved and some poor judgment from many different quarters. Now that is behind us, or should be very shortly. I believe that at the time the problem should have been nipped in the bud but it was not. It was allowed to become a blunt and rather crude instrument for expressing our position to something proposed by the Government. Worse than that, it made the Canadian Parliament something of a laughing stock, a joke. Imagine having bells ring for days on end and Members of Parliament not coming to their seats to divide on a question which had been put to it? Whoever heard of such a practice?
The provision for the ringing of bells had always existed so that Members of Parliament, under certain difficulties, bad weather or having to travel great distances, could get back for a vote. Sometimes there were reasons for the bells to ring for many hours but it had more to do with geography than with opposition to a particular proposal before the House.
Perhaps even worse than those items I have mentioned, the long bells became a precedent for others. I remember being in the province of Manitoba at a time when that Parliament was in the midst of a bell ringing crisis. The issue was the extension of linguistic rights to the Francophone minority of Manitoba
and I arrived there for a parliamentary conference in the midst of the ringing of the bells.
We now have a proposal for up to a 30 minute bell, and it does not have to be that long. If there were some good reason why the division could not take place, if, for example, we had a minority Parliament and Members of Parliament were caught in a snowstorm in Toronto and could not arrive for the vote and there was some danger that a Bill or other measure would be lost, there is an allowance in the proposed Standing Orders for the division to take place the following day before six o'clock. That is a plus for Parliament and for Hon. Members of this House.
Reference has already been made to the power of the Speaker to name a Member without having to seek a motion of the House. I entirely agree with the Opposition House Leader that when a Speaker names a Member for creating disorder, in fact the decision has already been made and the placing of a motion before the House simply delays getting on with the business of the House. It should be in the power of the Speaker to name that person and that person should, having been named, leave the House of Commons for the remainder of that day.
This particular rule among our Standing Orders is a vestige or remnant from the days when the Speaker's rulings could be appealed. That is now no longer possible except in this one case where a Member is being named. So we accept that proposal.
I would, however, say to the House Leader that 1 believe, along with many of my colleagues, that if the same Member is named on a subsequent occasion in the same session, it is excessive to ask that Member to leave the Chamber for a period of up to five days. That in my view is, or could be, an excessive penalty, and I would like the House Leader to perhaps consider that particular point.
I know that some of my colleagues have not been happy with legislative committees. I take a different view. I believe that the introduction of the system of legislative committees has been a positive step for this House and for Members of Parliament. It really means that standing committees, which now have their own work schedule agreed to among the various Members of the Parties in the committee, will not have their work schedule interfered with by having a Bill introduced which they must deal with expeditiously. They will be able to carry on with their work schedule as they wish. The legislative committee can then focus its attention on a particular statute following second reading. It can insist that those public witnesses who appear before it come with specific matters related to the clauses in the Bill. I beleive that the chairmen, in co-operation with the clerk of those legislative committees, should be careful to instruct witnesses that they are not there to render broad and general briefs about the state of the nation. They are there to talk about that Bill. I believe that the chairman of the legislative committee should call the witness to order if he or she ranges widely over many subjects.
The concern of my colleagues has been that we are over-taxing the legislative committee system. There are too many. We
February 11, 1986

need a traffic control system. 1 am not going to dwell on that. Members on the Government side have made the same point. It is not something which needs to be put into our Standing Orders. It is a matter of some sort of scheduling system which can be worked out among the House Leaders.
I am also pleased with the Standing Order which states that parliamentary secretaries will no longer be members of standing committees. I believe that very frequently when standing committees look at a particular issue or problem to which they have agreed they will study for a particular period of time, that partisanship tends to subside and to be put into proper perspective and the issue or problem becomes paramount. These committees become what I would describe as "issue oriented". The parliamentary secretary certainly has a role in the legislative committee, because it is a Government Bill in most cases and he or she would want to be there to protect the position of the Government. However, I believe, we want to reduce the level of partisanship in the standing committee and have it involve itself more in important public policy issues. The parliamentary secretary would have less of a role there than he would in the legislative committees.
I would also like to say that it is a plus for committees to be able to review Order in Council appointments. We all recognize that in a parliamentary system-and this is not a congress but a parliament-that we do not have the power of a veto. I think it is a great step forward to have a committee examine an appointee for competence. That will help in a great way to discourage the more unsavoury and objectionable aspects of patronage.
I will simply conclude with two brief points. First, I am delighted that this is an experimental approach to changing our Standing Orders. We will see how it works. There are bound to be some problems and difficulties. There is now a Procedure and Organization Committee to which Members of Parliament can refer difficulties and problems as they go along. But having carried out the work of an important parliamentary reform committee and having implemented some of those recommendations and Standing Orders, once they are approved, no one in this House should believe our task is finished. The reform of Parliament has to be what is sometimes referred to as "an ongoing process". I think we have to continue to attempt to improve that which we are doing. We have to continue to examine our procedures, asking at all times those very basic questions, is it good for Parliament? Does it make Parliament a more effective instrument for serving the public's well-being? Can we represent our constituents better? Can we do a better job for this nation?
If we keep those ideals in mind when we get to the practical aspects such as amending our Standing Orders and changing the administrative arrangements, I believe that over a period of time we will have a Parliament in which Members can take a great deal more pride. As well, those who watch us will be able to say that Parliament is serving them well.

Mr. Speaker, 1 do understand that an effort is being made to have as many members of the committee as possible comment on this report. Since I was not a member of the committee, I hope Members will accept that I have a serious interest in the issue of parliamentary reform. I support the fact that progress has been made in the discussions among the House Leaders of the three Parties and that some of the difficulties which were perceived when the matter was discussed with the caucuses have been resolved, allowing this piece of parliamentary reform to go forward.
I think the members of the McGrath committee should be congratulated for the work they have done. I hope that people across Canada recognize that this is part of a genuine effort by the House of Commons to move forward and to respond to the criticism of people who say that we are redundant, stuck in the mud, or cannot come to grips with the problems we will face in the future.
I was looking at the report of the Macdonald Commission today. It talks about the need for flexibility and the need to be more adaptable to change. I do not agree with a lot of its remedies, but I think the problem it describes is a very valid one. I think that the House of Commons, an institution of which I am a recent Member, but nonetheless for which I have a great deal of respect, must be able to adapt to change. I hope that this is the beginning of a process of change rather than the final episode.
In speaking to people in the country I find it difficult to explain what we do. This could be remedied by greater television coverage. It is difficult to explain to the public why only 30 or 40 Members of the House are here discussing this particular and important issue. Most of the other Members, I hope all of them, are in fact working right now in their constituencies, in committees, attending meetings with groups, doing work on behalf of their political Parties, which is part of their job, handling correspondence, and so on. Members are working even when they are not in the House of Commons, but that is often difficult to explain.
If the House is seen as degenerating into an overgrown kindergarten, as constantly bogging down because of the use of the rules to ring the bells and bring proceedings to a halt, or to engage in what the public views as procedural obfuscation, and, on the other hand, if the House or its committees are not seen as coming to grips substantively with important issues such as equality for women, the impact of technological change and the future of multicultural minorities, then we will become increasingly irrelevant and increasingly perceived as being unworthy of the many millions of dollars spent every year in order to maintain the Parliament of Canada.
I want to read one section from the proposed draft rules. 1 recognize that these may have changed a bit. It seems to me that this is one of the most important parts of the changes which are now taking place. This package contains some things which would enable the Government to speed up some proceedings of the House. It contains some measures which private Members want, such as the provision for Private

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
Members' Bills to be voted upon even without unanimous consent. The fact that the passage of the Private Members' Bill of the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCros-san), which relates to reporting of public pension funds, was such a rare occurrence indicates that that private Members' procedure was bogging down. That matter was under anxious discussion over the course of the last few weeks.
According to the draft Standing Orders, the standing committees will have the following role and mandate: They will be empowered to study and report on all matters relating to the mandate, management, and operation of the Department or Departments of Government which are assigned to them from time to time by the House. In general, the committees shall be severally empowered to review and report on the statute law relating to the Department assigned to them, the program and policy objectives of the Department and its effectiveness in the implementation of same, the immediate, medium, and longterm expenditure plans and the effectiveness of implementation of same by the Department, and an analysis of the relative success of the Department as measured by the results obtained as compared with its stated objectives. It goes on to mention other matters relating to the mandate, management, organization, or operation of the Department as the committee deems fit.
That is a wide-ranging addition to the powers of the standing committees. My experience in the Ontario Legislature before I came to this House was that the Estimates procedure was sufficiently prolonged that it allowed the kind of study which is consigned to committees in these Standing Orders with regard to Estimates. Under federal procedures the Estimates process does not permit that. Often the Minister, the deputy minister, and the other senior officials of a Department may only appear before a committee for one or two sessions, for perhaps five or six hours. That is simply not enough time to study the role and mandate of a Department, its program and policy objectives, its relative success, its long-term expenditure plans, etc.
The limitation of Estimates consideration in this House to a short period from the tabling of Estimates around the beginning of March until the end of May, also puts a constraint on what committees can do. Members find themselves running from one committee to another in order to raise a few regional issues which they did not have a chance to raise in the House of Commons. I believe that with smaller committees and a broader mandate we have the potential for having more powerful committees, which is one of the purposes of the reform.
I want to appeal to the people here in the House in the hopes that having that appeal on the record will have some influence on the future. The spirit of these reforms must be respected. In the Committee on Regional Development we had a fracas over how deeply we would look into the sale of de Havilland. We know from such experiences that the spirit of giving relatively free powers of inquiry and investigation to standing committees will be thwarted if government Members use their majority to prevent initiatives which will come from the Opposition. There will have to be some give and some take. I do not
pretend that everything the opposition Parties will want to do will be accepted, but there will have to be some acceptance of their initiatives. These initiatives must not be thwarted because a Parliamentary Secretary feels a bit uneasy, or the Minister does not like the committee poking around in what is going on in the Department or, God forbid, because a powerful deputy minister mutters between clenched teeth to get the committee off his back.
We are looking for ways of redressing the balance between a powerful executive and a powerful administration on the one hand, and a House of Commons which has had more and more difficulty in having its views enforced and in having a genuine influence on public policy. I have been around long enough to know that not every representation made by a committee, even one acting with unanimity, is going to be accepted by the Government or is going to have impact on the bureaucrats. However, many of those representations will have an impact, albeit delayed.
With regard to the spirit in which these reforms are going to be put forward, we must look at some of the practices of committees as well. When there is disagreement in a committee it should become a convention of the House to allow opposition Members more than a few lines in the committee report to express their point of view. There should be, de facto, a form of minority report which can be reflected in the report of the committee rather than Members having to communicate directly to the press. In order to work in the spirit in which these reforms came about, if difficulties are discerned in the next 11 months, the Government must not use its majority to stifle action to make changes where problems are perceived.
I would now like to take a few minutes to comment on one or two specific items. It is not clear whether standing committees will continue into the period of a new session or whether there will be a hiatus every January when a new session begins due to a rule which prevents committees from continuing because the Striking Committee will not have had a chance to meet.
I commend to Members the difficult experience we had with the Standing Committee on Regional Development which was seized with the matter of de Havilland before Christmas but then had to be rescued from oblivion by an agreement between the House Leaders at the eleventh hour on the final day before we rose for Christmas. If that had not occurred, the committee would not have been able to meet until the third or fourth week of January.
According to the old rules, beginning in January the committee did not exist until the Striking Committee recommended its coming into force, it had organized itself, chosen a chairman and finally got down to business. Without any assurance of being able to continue, we were unable to make arrangements for organizing witnesses prior to rising at Christmas, and that certainly contributed to some of the difficulty and confusion in the work of that committee.
February 11, 1986

If the rules do not address this situation I urge that they be changed so that next January or the beginning of the next session, the committees and their membership be prolonged until such point as the Striking Committee has recommended a new set of names and that report has been adopted by the House of Commons. That would ensure continuity for 365 days of the year.
I am pleased that legislative committees will not be required to have a minimum of 20 members. When one considers our other responsibilities, I hope that many legislative committees may be a lot smaller.
I believe that the requirements in the proposed Standing Orders that legislative committees be struck at the time of first reading will lead to confusion. Journalists will write that there is a proliferation of committees and that the traffic is too heavy. I believe two alternatives can be considered, if not now, then after a year's experience, in order to lighten the traffic of legislative committees.
First, we should agree that no more than a certain number of legislative committees should be working at one time. For example, perhaps the maximum number of legislative committees could be six. If there is a seventh or eighth piece of legislation before the House which has passed second reading, it should be put on hold until one of the six current inquiries has been concluded.
Second, I believe that the legislative committees should be struck at the time second reading is concluded rather than being struck after first reading. A 24-hour or 48-hour delay is all that is needed for the legislative committee to begin its work. If urgency is essential, there is no problem with the House Leaders or the Striking Committee informally deciding who is likely to be a member of the legislative committee when second reading is concluded. This would clear the Order Paper of lengthy lists of members of legislative committees that are not due to meet for many months, until the particular Bill that has been given first reading finally gets through second reading stage.
Third, on an experimental basis I think we should require the presence of Opposition Members for a quorum for a committee or, failing that, the consent of at least one opposition Member for a committee to work and act as though it has a quorum. For example, if no Opposition Member can be present for a meeting but agrees that the work of that committee can proceed where a quorum is required, I suggest that there should be written consent in the hands of the clerk at the beginning of a meeting.
I am concerned that section 78 will mean that committees will be open to misrepresentation with respect to their spending. These committees are faced with large amounts of fixed costs with respect to clerks and staff. As I mentioned in December, there is a cost of some $ 1,000 per staff person per meeting. Those are fixed costs rather than discretionary costs which the committee can control. While it is not in the Standing Orders, I suggest that this matter be considered in order that the committees be tagged with the discretionary costs that they have entailed and not with the fixed costs.
Standing Orders
I want to reiterate my concern about the scheduling matters. I hope that smaller committees will mean a great deal more flexibility as to when they meet so that there are not artificial distinctions which force them to meet in the evenings when I believe most committee members would prefer that they work during the day. Furthermore, I believe it is in the interest of public scrutiny that the press have access to the work of committees during the day.
The television arrangements should be revised quickly in order to permit a radio feed to committees and to allow selected committees, which may be selected in consultation with House Leaders, a committee of chairmen or the liaison committee, to meet in a committee room that can accommodate television cameras to record their operations. Those televised meetings could then be broadcast over the parliamentary channel, perhaps when the House of Commons is not meeting.
I have some real concern about the handling of questions. It is proposed that a Member have a right to no more than four questions on the Order Paper at any one time. The Table Officers are being given the right to decide whether a lengthy question should be divided, which means that a Member who thinks he or she has 4 questions may have 10 or 15 questions, depending on the discretionary decision of the Table Officers.
Members usually ask for a response within 45 days, which effectively means that over the course of a year a Member will have a right to a maximum of 35 questions if the Government answers within 45 days. If those questions are relatively short because of a decision by the Table in the interest of getting replies from the Government, I suggest we have unreasonably interfered with the right of opposition Members in particular to use the parliamentary question as a means of eliciting information from the Government. While I am not suggesting that this right be unlimited, one might consider giving an allotment of questions to a caucus in addition to the four questions per Member so that the caucus can decide if it wants to give further questions to a Member who has depleted his or her allotted questions. In any event, I suggest that more flexibility is needed in this area.
I also question the requirement that all petitions should be in a form which is acceptable to the Table and that they be first considered by the Table. I believe we are far too restrictive about petitions. If people want to say in simple words that they petition the House of Commons, that is all that is required for a petition to be acceptable. I am not against a requirement of 25 signatures or a minimum number of signatures, but we should not inhibit the public's right to petition Parliament by restricting them to medieval, anachronistic or archaic wording.
I hope that my arguments are helpful. I recognize they are of minor importance, but what is of material and major substance is that we are making a determined step forward in an attempt to reform this place. I hope that determination continues not just for the life of this Parliament but for the life that all of us hope to spend in this Parliament in future decades.

Are there any questions or comments?

February 11, 1986
