SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: Order. It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 46, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock)-Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-Broadcasting of song lauding suicide; the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault)- Textiles and Clothing-Commission's recommendations- Government position; the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry)-Corporate Affairs-Marketing of photographic developing machines.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate today-one for which I have been waiting for some time-and to review the work that has been done in the past as well as an opportunity to move ahead with some of the most significant reforms that have faced the Parliament of Canada.
Let me first begin by commenting briefly on the comments made by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). I was very pleased to hear the very positive approach he took to the report and to the initiative with which we are dealing today.
1 also want to thank my constituents for their patience in allowing me to work on this subject. When I first started
working on parliamentary procedure some five years ago, they found it a little difficult. They could not see immediate results and often questioned me about why I was spending so much time and effort on a subject that did not seem too practical.
What we see today is a demonstration of our commitment to this subject and to Parliament. We see the potential of the House of Commons, the potential of Members of Parliament and the potential that all of us have if we are given in which to work and the right kind of environment in which we can put forward ideas and suggestions. Hopefully we can make a positive contribution to our country.
I want to pay a tribute, as others have done, to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). As the Chairman of our special committee, there is no doubt he provided dynamic and aggressive leadership. I have to say that in my six years on the Hill it was a committee on which 1 have enjoyed serving more than any other committee. The work was very exciting. I enjoyed the debates and the strong, tough arguments that took place but not on a partisan basis. It was not at all uncommon to see the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and I together against the Chairman or someone else together with me against the Chairman. It was a group of Members who were trying very hard to put the best interests of Parliament and of their country before their own. It was the most exciting and dynamic experience of which I have ever been a part. I appreciated working with the Hon. Member for Papineau who represented his Party on the committee. His contribution was a very good and lively one.
I want to mention also the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) who represented the New Democratic Party. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) referred to the Hon. Member this morning. I thought it was significant that he recognized the work that the Hon. Member contributed to the committee.
Let me thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn). He had a tough go in the negotiations, but he stuck with us on the issue and, as a result, we have the debate today.
Last let me come to the Prime Minister. I sincerely believe that if it were not for his commitment to parliamentary and procedural reform, this debate would not be happening today. He stuck by us. He fought. He had tremendous courage throughout the debate and the discussions. I can remember the naysayer saying, when the report was first tabled, that the Prime Minister would never accept it, that he would never let it happen, that he would let it die.
But the Prime Minister did not let it die. He aggressively pursued the matter and encouraged the Hon. Member for St. John's East. He aggressively encouraged other members of the committee and Members of Parliament to pursue the issue and to get on with what he saw as a really important opportunity for parliamentarians.
The Prime Minister was willing, as he has admitted time and time again, to suffer some personal embarrassment to allow private Members or back-bench Members to stand up in
February 11, 1986

this House and make the kinds of motions and statements they want to make and to pursue legislation they want to see pursued. He feels that is the kind of Parliament we should have. I respect and admire his leadership on that issue.
I want to touch on some of the work that I particularly enjoyed and think is important. I do not mean in any way to diminish other parts of the report. I want to highlight the parts for which 1 have a particular fondness. The area of committee work is one. Since arriving on Parliament Hill, I have spent quite a bit of time in committees. I have found the committee work to be one of the most profitable areas for a Member to work in. So often we found ourselves frustrated by a system that was cumbersome and that made our work futile. Very often we did not feel we were accomplishing the kinds of things that we as Members of Parliament wanted to accomplish.
The first change this report recommends that 1 think is important is to give committees more freedom and scope to look into matters that concern them. They can also get more involved in the legislative and drafting process. That is significant. I know the time spent on that part of the committee review was spent in very serious discussion which had a lot of implications. We felt strongly that we wanted to see the committees in the Parliament of Canada play a much more dynamic and unique role in our institution.
Another element important to the committees was the ability to hire experts. Often, as committee members, we felt frustrated by the process. We did not feel that we were backed by adequate expert staff to deal with the experts we face on various issues. I am sure all of us at one time or another in committee have dealt with witnesses we did not feel qualified to question. As a result, some of our work has not perhaps been the kind of work we hoped would come forward. With this provision, Mr. Speaker, we will see some changes made to the committee process. The whole question of Order in Council appointments is significant. When we looked at this area we looked at what the Americans have done and how they have dealt with it. We felt strongly that in Canada we, as Members of Parliament, must have the right to look at the people who are receiving some of these very important positions, which affect the policy and the direction of our nation. Up to now these appointments have been made and this policy has been exercised with virtually no scrutiny by Parliament, with no questioning of competence, expertise or ability of the person called upon. With this change, we will see quite a difference in the type of appointments that come through.
Individuals who accept an appointment will know they may well face a scrutiny of their abilities and their talents. There will be more hesitation in accepting an appointment simply because of the salary, the status or whatever goes with a particular job. It is certainly our goal and my goal to see good quality people coming forward for jobs. People will be put under scrutiny, and we will have better people to fill these important roles.
Another area that affected the committees to a certain degree, certainly one committee of the House, was the whole
Standing Orders
business of reviewing regulations. Those have been a constant thorn in the side of Members of Parliament. Some Members have distinguished themselves over the years by looking into regulations. But they often faced frustration and futility. Now we will see some changes.
The committee wanted to see smaller committees. We wanted to see committees shrink in size. In today's bigger and better society, it seemed to be a little twist out of the ordinary, but my experience is that it is a good idea. The committee that drafted this report resulting in the motion we are dealing with today, was a small committee. One built very strong relationships with the people one worked with. This tends to break down partisan lines. We reinforced and encouraged each other to do better and more thorough work, even though in some cases it was a little uncomfortable. After the adjustment period through which all of us will have to go after the introduction of these new rules or new ideas, it will be one of the most significant changes. The net result will be that committee members will be trying hard to get on that particular committee and will be struggling to keep their membership.
I think we will see better work as a result.
Another area which has been fairly topical today is that of written questions. It has been a constant frustration for Members of Parliament on all sides of the House to have to sit around and wait for an answer which may or may not ever come. It begins to feel like something one does to use up a little time and pass the day. None of us want to waste our time that way. I am pleased to see those changes coming forward.
I should like to refer to a situation in the last Parliament which struck me as being somewhat frustrating. One of our Members died and, after a period of time, there was no office or staff on the Hill to represent his constituents. As a result, neighbouring Members of Parliament tried to pick up the work. However, the truth of the matter was that constituents in a riding in Canada had no representation in the House of Commons for a considerable time. That has happened in the past, and I think it must cause all of us as Members of Parliament some concern. I am pleased to see that we are extending the staff provisions for six months so that constituents will have a chance to come to an office and talk about their concerns. No one should be in a position of having nowhere to go or having to know someone else to deal with. Although it is a very small reform in some ways, it will mean a significant difference to a number of people if such circumstances arise again.
Mr. Speaker, you have been given much needed power in terms of the disciplining of Members. I am sure the Speaker will find that power to be difficult to use at times and will be somewhat uncomfortable. However, the truth of the matter is that we feel very strongly that the Speaker, in order to establish authority in the House of Commons, has to be able to do something without relying on someone else to pass a motion or an amendment. Throughout history Speakers have been left in rather uncomfortable positions at times, and we certainly do

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
not want to see a repeat of that. This is why we went ahead with the provision. It will be a difficult situation. References were made earlier this morning to some of the implications and some of the dangers. Members of Parliament elect the Speaker because we have confidence in the individual. This means we will also have confidence in his or her ability to use that new power.
Another area which has been much talked about over the last little while is the whole area of confidence. It was one area with which we as a committee found it difficult to come to grips. I am sure most Hon. Members know that we ended up having a discussion about it but not making a direct recommendation in the report in that particular area. We want to see the whole concept of confidence being removed except in extreme cases such as the Budget and particular Bills or laws which are important to the Government of the day. We wanted to see an ability on the part of Members of Parliament to vote according to their consciences and on behalf of their constituents from time to time. We wanted to see that practice develop a little. Of course it is the kind of thing which will be an uncomfortable transition for Members of Parliament. We can change the rules, but to change attitudes is another story. There has been a very strong hesitancy on the part of Hon. Members over the last little while to vote against their Parties, and for very obvious reasons. The minute Members do that, they are targeted in the press as mavericks or as being at odds with their Party or with the leadership of their Party. As a result, Members who may have felt very strongly about a particular issue were not prepared to take those kinds of risks. In order for this to come about, there will have to be a change in the attitude of each of us in this institution. There will have to be a change as well in the attitude of the Government or of the Cabinet of the day. In addition, there will have to be a change in the attitude of the press to ensure that it does not set up the individual as some kind of martyr or maverick who is about to take on his Party and fight his leadership. If we really want to see the free vote come to Parliament, it can only come when it is accepted as a legitimate role and responsibility of a Member of Parliament in certain circumstances.
I should like to talk for a couple of minutes about a subject of which I am very fond, that is, the whole area of Private Members' Business. When I was elected to the House, I felt strongly that I could do some positive things or take some positive action, not simply sit back and respond to the legislation placed before me or react to the debate which someone else put on the table. I wanted to be able to play some kind of role or to take some kind of leadership in the issue. With these new private Members' provisions, for the first time we as Members of Parliament have a real opportunity to do that. The first thing we will do is to have our Bill selected in the draw. Then we take the motion or Bill we want debated before a committee of our peers, Members of Parliament. Then we argue why our particular Bill should come to a vote. I love the dynamics of that. I love the opportunity for Members of Parliament to appear in front of a group of back-benchers, such as the individual who is making the presentation, and say
that the issue is an important one and why they think it should go forward. The decision will be made by our peers, the very people with whom we work in this institution, the very people who are faced with many of the same problems and frustrations. I see it as a very dynamic opportunity. It will change our attitude toward the House of Commons and our attitude toward the kinds of things we want to accomplish.
It was made clear this morning that it puts tremendous responsibility upon the members of the committee. The members who will be making the decisions will be faced with some very tough ones. They will have to decide the criteria upon which they want to make a decision. The decision cannot be based upon personal attitude or upon personal ideas about a particular Bill. They will have to look at more than that.
I see that my time is running out, but I should like to refer to the idea that I can now have a Bill come to a vote in the House of Commons. I am not faced with standing and making a speech, only to know that no one is listening, no one cares and no action will be taken on it. I feel that for once there will be an opportunity to make a contribution, to put something forward and to see it come to some sort of resolution. This does not guarantee that I will win, but it gives me a chance to see something I have done come to a vote. As a result, Members of Parliament will now have a much more direct influence upon what goes on. They will be able to provide some leadership. They will be able to test some of their important ideas. They will be able to do a number of significant things.
I should like to touch quickly upon something that I mentioned earlier. It has been said that one can reform the asylum but that it is tough to change the inmates. That is what we are faced with. We can make the kinds of changes to the institution we want, but until those reforms really become a part of what we are doing, we have a real problem on our hands. There is a change in responsibilities.
The first change will affect Members of Parliament. If we do not make those changes in attitude and use our new freedom and influence, there is no point in changing the Standing Orders. Second, the Government or the Cabinet has to respect the input and ideas of individual Members of Parliament, because it may find that those individuals with new influence and power can suddenly put pressure upon the Government. I think it will change the dynamics of the way in which Parliament works. Third, as I mentioned briefly before, the press itself will have to change the way it looks at Members of Parliament working in the House.
The most important thing that I can say is that this is a significant day for Parliament. We are seeing changes that are profound and that will change this institution and the way we think about ourselves and about our role as Members of Parliament. I am looking forward to passing this motion and stepping into the new period, the transition and the test time, to have the kind of Parliament that I think all of us hope for, dream for and work for.
February 11, 1986

The Hon. Member talks about attitudes being the tool which will bring the new changes that he foresees in Parliament. I wonder if he could elucidate for us what he sees the role of Cabinet to be in this particular new system. If you look at some of the recommendations in the original McGrath Report, for example, on the issue of Order in Council appointments, you will find that the commission suggested that Order in Council appointments would be subject, not only to review, but also to a decision-making process through Members of parliament, that is, if Members themselves did not agree with the specific appointment they would have the power to overturn that appointment.
I could be wrong and perhaps the Chairman could elucidate this further for me, but in the current Bill that is before us we have the power of review, however, there is no power to overturn a Cabinet decision. Frankly, I think that if we believe that this particular document is going to lead to a parliamentary reform, in essence we are buying a pig in a poke, because we do live in a parliamentary system. The Cabinet, the executive of the asylum, remains the same. The ordinary inmate may in fact be more democratized in the process, but as long as we have a Cabinet that is the bottom line, and a Cabinet that is the chief decision-making corpus of the asylum, then the heart, the soul and the guts of the asylum remain untouched. Maybe I am a little more cynical than others, but I think that, as long as we are governed by the parliamentary process and governed by the Cabinet process, this notion of attributing more power to private Members is, indeed, an illusory notion. 1 would hate to think that we would be making all of our efforts in parliamentary reform with the illusory notion that more power is being given to the private Member. I think that more power to the Private Member will not accrue from this particular Bill because we are still stymied by the role and the authority vested in Cabinet, and specifically in the Prime Minister's Office. I wonder how this Bill addresses those specific concerns?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to try to address the Hon. Member's comments for a moment, if I can. First of all, I want to start where she left off. She said that she does not see this particular motion changing the dynamics or the role of a private Member of Parliament. I can say that, after having worked on this report, having spent five or six years looking at what happens here, I think we are facing more significant changes to the role of a private Member of Parliament than we have ever seen in the Canadian House of Commons.
Now, if we talk about the committees' role, for example, the advantages that the committees have; the expanded power, the expanded ability to look into subject areas, the expanded ability to hire expert staff, the expanded ability to go ahead with the kind of work that I think is important, those are the kinds of things that really will change the dynamics of Members of Parliament in this institution, that is, to go back to the specifics that the Hon. Member referred to, the veto power of a committee in dealing with Order in Council appointments. I should point out that, as I recall it, in the original report there were some 64 appointments that would be subject to veto.
Standing Orders
Now those have been changed. A colleague from her own Party, I think it was the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) talked about this particular subject at length. One of the comments he made-and I think it is a very relevant one-is that we are not in a Congressional system where you have the difference between the executive versus the Congress, and as a result the executive can make the appointment, but we have the opportunity to review it. The question that I put to the Member is this: If the Cabinet comes forward with a recommendation for an appointment but then that particular individual receives a highly critical and negative report from the committee, then I think it would have the same impact and the same power as a veto itself. Even though we could have gone to that extent-and we did talk about it in our original report, but there were some dangers to that, as was mentioned by her colleague from Cochrane-Superior-in fact, with this kind of an opportunity to come forward with a negative report or a critical examination of an individual, we are taking a very dramatic step forward, and certainly a step that I know very, very few people on the street expected to see taken. So we have made significant progress. This is a dramatic change. We are going to have time to test it, we are going to have time to see how it works, but it is certainly a step in the right direction, and I am sure the Member herself would not deny that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Hon. Member. I have a press report here that quotes the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It reads as follows:
It's true that he makes fine speeches and I really like him. His media relationships are more distant, more sporadic. He doesn't have to face the House of Commons every day. It's an almost ideal situation.
The person quoted is the Right Hon. Prime Minister, and of course he is referring to President Ronald Reagan. It would suggest to me that the Prime Minister does not hold our system in high esteem. I would like to ask the Member who spoke for the Government about certain comments made by the Prime Minister during his speech just before the lunch hour. As he knows, the Prime Minister made a very rare appearance in the House to make a speech. He appeared at ten to one, knowing, of course, that the House would adjourn at one o'clock, and then did not reappear at three o'clock in order to give Government Members and other private Members an opportunity to question him.
I would like to ask the Member if the Prime Minister is truly serious about enhancing the role of the private Member, and if he is really sincere about parliamentary reform, why would he say that the President of the United States has an almost ideal situation because he does not have to face the House of Commons every day? Why would he not come back to the House in order to answer questions from private Members? Would you not agree with me that his actions lead one to question his credibility seriously?

Mr. Speaker, I am really glad that the Member has asked me this question because it really gives me an opportunity once again to talk about the role of the Prime Minister in the reform package that is before us today. If this

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
Member had taken the time and looked back-he may well have done that-on the history of the reform of the Parliament of Canada, he will know that it is very rare for a Prime Minister to make a commitment and to take the time and have the energy to bring about real reform. This particular Prime Minister has never hesitated, from the day that the motion came forward in this House, to establish the McGrath task force. He has continued steadfastly to make commitments and statements in public about the importance of reform. He has pushed it and prodded it and kept it going until we ended up debating the motion here today. I do not remember the last time that I saw a Prime Minister come in and take part in a debate in the House of Commons without being the lead speaker. In other words, the Prime Minister came in here today, sat in his place and spoke as another Member of Parliament very much concerned about the whole process of parliamentary procedural reform. He talked about the importance and the dynamic need for Members of Parliament, private Members of Parliament, back-bench Members of Parliament, to take part in what is going on.
There is an old expression which says that actions speak louder than words. The Member has been around here long enough to know that from time to time quotations that appear in newspapers, on the radio or on television, are not necessarily in context, are not necessarily accurate. The thing that really counts, and it counts to every Member that is in this House of Commons, is not so much what we say but the actions. The Prime Minister, more than any other parliamentarian, has demonstrated his desire and his fight for real reform in Canada.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): I want to start by saying that I do not believe that everything in the package of rule changes before us is reform, and consequently to oppose some of these items is not to oppose reform. I would say about two-thirds of the package of rule changes is good, and I would describe it as reform, and I am ready to support it. However, some major proposals in the package were not even recommended by the special committee of which the Hon. Member who just spoke was a member.
As the Hon. Member and others have said, we can make all the changes in the rules that we like, but if the attitude of the Members with respect to those rules does not change, we will not have much meaningful reform. If the attitude of the Government with respect to the role of Parliament does not change and if the attitude of government back-benchers and opposition Members does not change, we are not going to see very much reform despite the technical changes to the rules that have been proposed today.
We know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and some of the Ministers very often make great rhetorical statements about this or that, but they end up doing exactly the opposite. It was very surprising to read in the newspaper this morning that the Prime Minister said yesterday that, in his opinion, the President of the United States is in the ideal
situation because he does not have to go to Parliament. The Prime Minister came to the House today to make a speech in this debate to try to counteract the negative statement he made yesterday, but it indicated to me that he really does not know what this is all about. He is for parliamentary reform, but when very real situations arise in which parliamentary reform should be applied, it is not being applied.
We did not see parliamentary reform applied with respect to the closure of the Gulf refinery in the East of Montreal. We wanted to have that issue examined by a parliamentary committee, but that did not happen. As a matter of fact, the decision was made by one Minister, almost in contradiction with several other Ministers and Members of Parliament from Montreal who were very closely related to the problem at hand, and there was no examination by Parliament. We did not even see the documents that were prepared by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs touching on that issue, documents which Members of Parliament needed to discuss the matter fully. The same thing happened with de Havilland. We had to push and fight with the Government to get that matter examined by a parliamentary committee. Finally the Government agreed to it, but then it went off and made the decision even before the parliamentary committee had a chance to report.
Just today I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) if he would make no decision with respect to the transfer of commercial jet flights to Mirabel until a committee of the House has had a chance to examine all the options and to consult with the public in Montreal on those options. He would not make such a commitment. The Minister said that the Government, in its wisdom, would do what it had to do and would make a decision. With those kinds of answers to specific questions, one wonders what is really meant by the Government talking about parliamentary reform. As I said, a lot depends on the attitude of all Members on the Government side and on the Opposition side.
I indicated previously that I thought that about two-thirds of the package was good. I think the proposals with respect to petitions are good. In the past, when we presented petitions on behalf of our constituents, we never knew if the Government was going to answer them. Our constituents often asked us what had happened to the petitions we presented in Parliament with respect to family allowances, de Havilland or other issues. The new rule change will oblige the Government to give us some kind of reply.
I also like the proposals with respect to the Private Members' Business. I think it is very good that Private Members' Business will be given more attention and that six Bills will be allowed to proceed to a vote. However, I do have some reservations about which I put questions this morning to the Hon. House Leader. We will be testing this procedure over a number of months. We will have to wait to see how the new standing committee on Private Members' Business chooses the six Bills that will come to a vote. We will want to see if it chooses only those Bills which will cause no problem for the Government or have no great issues associated with them or if
February 11, 1986

the Government will choose all Government-sponsored Bills or only Bills regarding one subject matter. I am willing to give that a chance. On the whole, I think the proposals for private Members' Business are good ones.
I think that the proposals for written questions are good ones and 1 think that the proposal to limit the bells is a good proposal. I would like to remind the House that the abuse of the bells was not started by this Opposition Party but by the Party now in government-
Oh, wait a minute!

I was here, my dear friend. While we may have repeated it, we never repeated it to the extent it was used when it was first started. I was here when those bells rang night and day for almost two weeks. That was an abuse and I am glad to see that the rules will be changed to bring that abuse to an end. There has to be another way to oppose the Government when it is hell bent on destruction and on doing something the Opposition thinks is wrong other than ringing the bells forever.
I also agree with the proposal that allows the Speaker to suspend a Member for a day when the Speaker names him for misbehaviour without the requirement for a vote of the House. 1 do not think that a vote of the House should be necessary. We abolished appeals on Speaker's rulings a few years ago, and 1 think it is logical that we abolish the vote on suspending Members for a day when the Speaker names them. On the other hand, although that is quite a step forward, I do not agree that we should be allowed to suspend a Member for up to five days for a second infraction. Perhaps there should be a stiffer penalty for a second infraction, but I am not willing to jump that far in one set of amendments. Let us see how the new rule works. If it works well, then at the end of the trial period we could consider something for those who misbehave more than once in a Session.
Those are some of the good things about the proposals. Now I will mention some of the proposals that I do not believe to be reform. Up until today, I have not been convinced and I am still not convinced, having listened to the debate, that legislative committees spell reform. No one has been able to convince me that by having another layer of committees called legislative committees, we have reformed the House. I would like to relate to the House the experience I had with a legislative committee in the last month.
The legislative committee dealing with Bill C-62, the Bill for employment equity, was composed of 20 Members of Parliament. There were two from the Liberal Party, two from the NDP and 16 from the government Party. During the hearing of witnesses, there were usually between five and six government Members and two or three opposition Members present. There was a core of Government Members and opposition spokesmen who were present for the hearing of witnesses.
Once we began the clause-by-clause voting on the Bill, almost the entire committee was present. However, a large number of Government Members who had never heard witnesses and did not know what the Bill was about sat in and
Standing Orders
simply voted against amendments put forward by Opposition Members without any consideration of what was said during the hearing of evidence and without any consideration of what our arguments were. As a matter of fact, during the clause-byclause voting on that Bill, only three Government Members, the Parliamentary Secretary, the Chairman of the standing committee and one other Member, were au courant with the Bill and the issues. As well, there were two members of the NDP and two members of the Liberal Party who had gone through the whole process. There were as many abuses in that legislative committee as there were in the standing committees a number of years ago when the Party in power simply changed the members present at every meeting and shoved them in simply to vote for the Government's clauses without any regard to the evidence as none or very few of them had heard that evidence.
That was my experience with a legislative committee. I do not consider that to be reform. I consider that to be reactionary and a step backward from what we were doing a number of years ago. People have said that Members of the House of Commons will be Fighting to get on these new standing committees, that they will be small and that they will be dealing with issues. To me, the principal work of the House is legislation. I will want to be on the legislative committees. I will not spend my time on standing committees studying some obscure issue. If there are legislative committees sitting, it will be important for me to sit on those committees. That is where the action will be. To lay a complete new layer of committees on top of the existing layer of standing committees is a mistake. It has not been demonstrated that this is reform. It is something based on the supposition that a certain number of Members on a standing committee will be studying some important questions relating to, for example, employment, and there will be another set of Members examining a Bill put forward by the Minister of Employment and Immigration on employment equity, let us say. It is proposed that there be two completely different sets of Members dealing with the issue and that they will be able to work at the same time. However, that is not possible in a House which has just 262 Members. It might be possible in Great Britain where there are over 600 Members and where the number of legislative committees is limited to five at any one time. It will not be possible in our House of Commons. Not only have the opposition Parties with their small number of Members found it difficult to man standing committees and legislative committees, but even the Government with its large membership has found it difficult. As a matter of fact, the Government keeps rotating them around without really knowing what is going on, as I just pointed out with respect to the legislative committee on Bill C-62 which deals with employment equity.
We have seen the system working for a few months now. I do not think it has worked well. However, we are now going ahead in a somewhat more permanent way, although it is still not completely permanent. I am willing to bet that it will not work well unless a limit is placed on the number of legislative
10700

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
committees which can work at any one time, as is the case in Great Britain. There, pieces of legislation have to queue up to to go to one of these legislative committees. That, of course, slows down the process, but there are only a limited number of Members here to study all these issues and all these Bills. Legislation just cannot be proliferated. It cannot be expected that it will be given close attention by Members of Parliament and by community groups which want to comment on legislation which is before a committee. We cannot expect all that to happen with just 262 Members of Parliament. When we take out the members of the Government who sit in Cabinet, and there are about 30, the Chief Government Whip and the Leaders of the Opposition Parties, we are left with a limited number of Members who must work in these committees. As a matter of fact, I met with a member of the Government this past week who told me that he comes to Ottawa only one day a week. He comes on his duty day and spends the other four days of the week in his riding. This is what he admitted to me. He said: "Why should I come to Ottawa? I am not going to sit in those committees and never say anything or do anything. I get more done in my constituency". I really do not know about that situation. We are elected to be legislators. One hopes that if we were to have real reform, then people such as that would have a role to play.
I would now like to deal with the new rule with respect to examining Order in Council appointments in committee. When the Prime Minister first made his promise on the matter during the election campaign I thought he was proposing something similar to the American system. However, what has been put to us for consideration is that we consider the appointment after the fact, after it has been made. I am wondering what this will amount to. After all, the person will have been appointed already as, let us say, Chairman of the National Parole Board or President of Air Canada, and we will then call that person to appear before the committee and examine him. 1 think what we will find out is that Government Members will defend the appointment no matter what. Likely, members of the Opposition will attack the person if he or she does not have the proper qualifications. However, if the appointee has the qualifications, then the time of the committee will not be wasted by calling that person before it. What can members of the committee do? Make a report that the appointment was not a good one? Will Government Members really do that the closer we get to elections? I doubt it. I do not consider that much of a reform either.
I would now like to deal with the proposal in regard to the declaration of interest by members of Parliament, and especially the requirement to list trips which we take abroad. I am quite willing to list all the trips that I take, not only those sponsored by non-parliamentary associations and by my political Party but all of them. In putting forward this proposal I do not know why the Government has not made it necessary to include all trips which are taken by Government Members with their Ministers to conferences such as those held by the OECD, the ILO or all sorts of other ones which are held around the world. We frequently see planes flying off with two
or three Government Members. Now and then a member of the Opposition will be taken along, but that is a rare occurrence. Why not make it a requirement to declare all these trips? By the way, this proposal did not come out of the special committee chaired by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I believe it must have come out of the office of the Government House Leader, or somewhere else.
It was proposed in committee that there be more votes which would not be considered votes of confidence. That means that the House could vote on certain matters and defeat a clause in a Government Bill, or even defeat a Government Bill, without putting the Government in jeopardy and without having the Government resign because of the defeat. If the rules were changed in that respect, then it would be more likely that Members would express themselves as they really believe the issue dictates and not simply as their Whips want them to. There is nothing in the package of proposals that is before us on that issue.
It is said that the new standing committees will be free, that they will conduct in-depth studies and issue reports in which will be put forward what the committees really believe should be done. I have my doubts in this respect. If those reports are made to the House and are subject to a motion for concurrence, then Members can always move concurrence in the report of a standing committee, for example on employment and immigration, and I can move concurrence in the report of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, but the majority of Members on those committees will not feel free to make reports which are contrary to Government policy, despite what they have heard from witnesses in committee. If this is the case then there will be no free vote; or a vote on such reports would involve confidence in the Government when concurrence is moved and voted upon. We will be watching this matter during the trial period to see if there is any movement in that direction.
Finally, I was disappointed to see that there is no provision for televising the proceedings of committees. I think this would help the work of committees and give them more importance. If the proceedings were televised, then some of the focus would be taken off the House, especially Oral Question Period.
To conclude, as far as I am concerned the opinions of Members of Parliament with respect to rule changes are not just a matter of party policy. It is something that affects every individual Member of Parliament. I think the rules should be such that they allow Members to dissent from their Parties and still have some provision in the rules for them in doing that. To push my thinking a bit further, I do not think we should make any rules today which would not provide well in a minority Parliament. In the 20 years in which I have been here there have been, I believe, four minority Parliaments. In the first one there were four Parties in opposition and it took only two of those Parties to join together to defeat the Government. On another occasion there were three Parties in opposition, and in another Parliament there were two. When we formulate our rules we must do so in such a way that all those people who are elected will have a fair and equitable chance to
February 11, 1986

participate in debate and to raise their side of the issue. In my opinion that is the real goal of reform.
I think the purpose of Parliament should be to discuss the important issues of the country at length. There should be an opportunity for all sides of the question to be put forward, and then we should vote. We should not debate the matter forever, although it should not be rammed through. There should be an opportunity for debate and an opportunity for all sides of the issue to be made public. In formulating the rules in this respect I do not think we can focus on just the Government Party and on the Official Opposition, or the fact that those two Parties are run completely by either the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition. There has to be room for the individual Member to express himself in opposition to his Party when he wants to do so. That is Parliament. We are all elected in our constituencies by electors who elect us to Parliament for specific reasons.
I agree with about two thirds of what is in this package. There are some important proposals with which I do not agree. I would hope that the Government House Leader and Government Members would reconsider some of the points they have put before us. If they really do believe in parliamentary reform, they should certainly not ram this package through. It should be subject to a wider range of opinions. Our House Leader has been involved in consultations, as well as other House Leaders, but I think this is something that needs more consideration.
Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) and then the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie).

I rise on a point of order. With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I think if you read the rules with respect to the time for questions or comments, you will see that it is incumbent on the Chair to recognize a member of a Party other than that of the Member who just spoke, if such Members are rising, which I am doing.
I appreciate the Hon. Member's point. It is not in the rules that way, but it has sometimes been our practice.
It is in the rules.

No, it is not. What I have been doing today is making no assumptions about Party on the assumption that we were talking about matters of parliamentary reform and that Hon. Members would want me to do that.
However, since earlier two questions were put by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East and the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata), I am sure the Hon. Member for Hamilton East is prepared to wait and allow the first question to be put by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie).
Standing Orders

I just wanted to say one thing very briefly, Mr. Speaker. I was glad that the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) concluded his speech by speaking about the kind of Parliament he would like to see, because if I had to do the very dangerous thing of singling out any Member of Parliament who, I believe, over the years has embodied the kind of Member of Parliament of whom we want to see more as a result of this reform, then it would be the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East. As a government Member, he was known on many occasions to have expressed an opinion different from that of his Party and to have voted differently from his Caucus. He has acted in this Parliament with the kind of integrity and independence of judgment of which we would like to see more in this place.
That is what the Liberal Party is all about.

Well, that is another matter. What I would like to say is that I hope the Hon. Member could see his way clear to supporting the package, with that in mind.
With respect to the point he raises about legislative committees, I hope that very soon someone from the Government side will rise and say that this matter of putting a limit on the number of legislative committees which can sit at any time is a legitimate issue. It is not a big deal. It is something we can handle by mutual agreement. For God's sake, let someone get up and say that that can be done so that this is no longer an issue.
I think the Hon. Member should also admit for the record that he has not liked the idea of legislative committees from the beginning, and this is part of the problem. It is not something new that has come up as a result of our experience with it. I think he did not like them in principle, to begin with. But I hope the Hon. Member will give them a chance under the ideal conditions, that is, under the conditions which the committee had in mind. We have not really tried them under those conditions. We have tried them in rather anomalous conditions. I hope the Hon. Member would give them a chance to work as we conceive them; then if his criticisms persist, so be it.

Mr. Speaker, we are willing to give them another chance to prove themselves. I hope, as the Hon. Member suggested, that someone will get up to say that no more than five legislative committees will sit at the same time because I think that is what they have in Britain.
Eight in Britain.
Is it eight in Britain? Well, they have over 600 Members.
No, no, six.
Well, they have eight slots.

Five or six would be reasonable here. Let me say that the reason I opposed them in principle at the beginning was that I felt that if we develop a number of Members

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders
who become expert in transport, external affairs, defence, employment or the environment, then why should we then decide to send a piece of legislation dealing with that very same subject to another group of Members who are not experts and have not studied those issues? The answer I have received so far is that those people on the standing committee can then all go over and sit on the legislative committee. If that is the case, I wonder then why have the two sets of committees?
We will need more experts, Warren. You will have to distribute the expertise. You can't be the only expert forever.
However, I am willing to give it a chance.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to speak in a non-partisan way, and I echo the comments made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). I must say, however, that I was in committee with another member of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), who said that as far as he was concerned, he did not intend to participate in committees with very few members because he thought it was a waste of his time. He did not see that the job would get done in small numbers. So I believe there is probably a fair degree of concern in all Parties as to how the new committee structure is going to work with 28 potential committees operating.
I would like to ask a couple of specific questions about rule changes as they relate to two issues which are obviously of concern to every Hon. Member. First, with respect to the issue of naming of Members, in the Standing Order we have in front of us, or the projet de loi, it is suggested that the Speaker be given the power to name a Member without necessarily calling a vote on the first occasion. On the second occasion, he can eject a person who is named for one week. I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether he agrees with that proposal since that was not the intention of the McGrath committee?
The second question, I think, relates to private Members' rights with respect to Standing Order 22. Under the current system, all Hon. Members are allowed 90 seconds for a statement under Standing Order 22. It is suggested that that be reduced to 60 seconds, with the intention of hearing more Hon. Members. However, it seems to me that if we are talking about the rights of private Members, and if we are concerned about giving more private Members an opportunity to speak, then we should abandon the current system of having a sort of perceived quota for each Party. For example, in the first 15 minutes of Question Period, approximately six statements under Standing Orders are made by the Government Party, three statements are made by the Liberal Party and two are made by the New Democratic Party. It seems to me that if we are really abandoning the notion of party policy, the statements under Standing Order 22 should be accorded on the basis of the people who are there and their own involvement and interests. I think if you will look at the record, Mr. Speaker, you will find that it has been members of the Liberal Party who have consistently stood up in large numbers on
statements under Standing Order 22. Unfortunately, it is the same Members of the Government Party who again and again rise on those statements. I wonder if the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) could comment on the possibility of throwing aside party lines when it comes to the issue of Standing Order 22 if the time for the statement is going to be reduced to only 60 seconds?

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I think that one minute is too short for statements under Standing Order 22. I would prefer 90 seconds. What I think will happen when we limit Hon. Members to 60 seconds is that all of their statements will be written and there will be no spontaneous statements spoken extemporaneously from one's seat because the Hon. Member will be fearful of being cut off before he gets his complete thought on the record. Everyone will write these statements down and more and more people will read their Standing Order 22. I think that is unfortunate. I agree with the principle of getting more statements under Standing Order 22 in, but I do not think it is a good idea to have them limited to one minute.
With respect to naming, I said in my remarks that I believe the Speaker should have the right to expel an Hon. Member when he names him or her without a vote of the House. However, I hesitate to agree with the new development of allowing the Speaker to expel an Hon. Member for up to five days on the second offence in a session. I would like to see us experiment for a trial period with this new procedure of the Speaker suspending a Member who is named for one day without a vote. If it works, then we can consider going to a tougher penalty on a second or third offence. 1 think we are going too far too fast without really knowing how it is going to turn out at this time, so I do not like the five-day provision at all.

speechtext: Order. The period provided for questions and comments has now expired. The Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault).

Mr. Speaker, if I could just comment briefly before I start my speech? I am sure that as far as the proposals by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), are concerned, the same could apply to Question Period, so it could be half and half. On this side of the House, we would have more time for putting questions to the Government if I follow the Hon. Member's-
Mr. Speaker, I am indeed delighted to be taking part in the debate on the proposed amendments to the Standing Orders, something we have been waiting for since September. Since I sat on the Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform, I am delighted to see that the Government has decided to support the Committee's recommendations.
February 11, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I must say that if anyone deserves the credit for today's debate and the fact that we are about to see a new Parliament, a new face with of course a change in attitude, the Prime Minister does. You know, when the boss says no, it is hard to change anything in a business. And the House of Commons is like a business. There is a boss, and the boss is the Prime Minister. 1 am sure he will not hold it against me if 1 reveal a caucus secret today, but the fact is that on several occasions in the Conservative caucus the Prime Minister did raise the issue of parliamentary reform. It is almost unheard of. This Prime Minister will rank high in the history of Canadian Prime Ministers because very seldom have we heard about a Prime Minister deciding just like that to transfer certain powers to Members of Parliament. I would suggest he deserves a round of applause from all of us.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I must say as well that the committee staff have worked closely with the committee members. I think those people deserve congratulations, because they are the ones who did all the research-including the deputy clerk-and followed the committee, and I can say that without them the committee would not have been able to do the outstanding job it did. I take this opportunity to thank and congratulate them. I am sure they are pleased today to see the Government going ahead with parliamentary reform.
Of course, I have to mention my committee colleagues. And then, Mr. Speaker, the staff have been very patient with me, for as a recently-elected Member every procedural question was something new to me. They were a great help. To them and to all my colleagues I express my appreciation and, I might as well confess, I have become an addict of parliamentary procedure. The chairman of our committee, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), kept us working very hard, but it was quite interesting. As I said before, I extend personal thanks to the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who acted as my translator and was of great help to me. Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am slightly upset over the official response of the Leader of the Opposition. We are talking about parliamentary reform, and the committee was responsible for finding ways to change the Standing Orders just so private Members would play a greater role. Indeed, we are now debating changes to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons because the special committee was given instructions by the Prime Minister to extend the powers of private Members.
I am somewhat disappointed to see that the Leader of the Opposition missed a good opportunity to say at last that it was not because he was on the Opposition side that he had necessarily to be against the Government, and perhaps the reverse is true. I suggest that we all have a sort of conscience to develop on this level. I must say that the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and the Hon. Member for
Standing Orders
Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) have in part contributed to lessen the impact made resulting from the reply given by the Leader of the Opposition. Mr. Speaker, his reply was, I felt, a little to partisan-oriented. The more so because for the first time the committee had heard the three party leaders as witnesses, and they were all in favour of these proposals. That is why I was rather disappointed with the answer given today by the Leader of the Opposition.
I am sure that the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) will arrange everything when he rises in the House tomorrow morning.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that my Argenteuil-Papineau constituents who watch only the Oral Question Periods, were quite disappointed recently with the lack of decorum. As a matter of fact, they said to me: It is the same as before. How is it that there are so many confrontations in the House of Commons? You just cannot... Well, that's the Parliamentary system. As the Prime Minister was saying, we are not going to change the Oral Question Period and the very biased approach of the various parties.
Personally, I told them that it is the part which presumably the House has to play, and that a lot of work is being done outside the Oral Question Period. But it is very frustrating to try to convince our constituents that we are working very hard, that there is more to parliament than the Oral Question Period. 1 had to tell them: "Personally, I sit on the Standing Committee on Agriculture and on the Committee of Transport, and I have all sorts of work and research to do in connection with that". In the past, when our constituents could not see us during the Oral Question Period, they felt that we were doing nothing in Parliament.
I feel, therefore, that the proposals to enhance the parts individual Members have to play will greatly justify the use of our time here.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that you will also be satisfied with the latitude you will enjoy from now on in procedural matters. You will therefore be able to set your own precedents and we shall not always be forced to refer to rulings made in the British House of Commons.
I think that, under the new Standing Order 1, Mr. Speaker, you will have the opportunity to give a Canadian character to this House and make typically Canadian rulings. In my opinion, this is long overdue.
As our servant, since, as you are always saying, you are the humble servant of this House, you will have increased powers under the new rules, and from now on, your authority will be recognized by the Members of this House. 1 am certain that you know what I mean, Mr. Speaker, by the word "authority", and the fact that you will now be the boss of the House of Commons, its true boss . . .

The Daddy!

February 11, 1986
Standing Orders

Yes, the Daddy.
Mr. Speaker, as a Government backbencher, I am also very pleased with the emphasis which will now be placed on Private Members' Business.
In French, we say "simple depute", while we say "private member" in English. In my opinion, it is not quite the same. The term "simple depute" does not really translate the notion of "private member". I simply want to point out in passing, Mr. Speaker, that we work for weeks trying to write a motion and have it debated and trying to convince the Government and our colleagues to support our views.
Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the House proposed a special debate on parliamentary reform some two months ago before presenting these amendments today, I took part in the debate and said that I was very curious about what happens to all the bills and motions moved by private members when, as we say in parliamentary language, they simply die on the Order Paper between 5 and 6 o'clock. The process is quite frustrating.
Mr. Speaker, I think that I am good at selling my ideas. I am interested in the role of voluntary work in our society and I have already proposed two motions in the House on this issue. I can tell you that, under the new rules, I shall rely on my personal staff and my selling ability to convince my colleagues of the Special Committee on Private Members' Business to accept my idea. If it is not accepted, I shall say, too bad, I cannot think that, just because I have introduced a bill, it is the best and is certain to be adopted. We have to be realistic. However, I shall still have the feeling that my bill can go further than with a one-hour debate and that it might have a chance of being referred to the committee for further study. This is something interesting which will benefit the Members of this House. I think that it will also benefit the Government, which will perhaps be able-
I see that you are looking at me, Mr. Speaker; has my time expired? Do I still have between five and ten minutes left?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT ADVISABILITY OF AWARDING EDUCATIONAL BURSARIES TO ATHLETES
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT ADVISABILITY OF AWARDING EDUCATIONAL BURSARIES TO ATHLETES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of awarding educational bursaries to members of teams who represent Canada at the amateur level in international competitions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, let me give some background before I deal with the motion before the House. I want to make clear at the outset that there are athletic assistance programs operating in Canada which use a system of A, B and C carded athletes. Carded athletes can depend on a certain amount of financial assistance to continue their university education.
The reason for my motion arises from my travels throughout my riding last summer. I went to a baseball tournament in Lac la Biche last summer at which a team representing Canada was made up of young athletes from across the country. I discovered that this team was hosting an international meet to be held in Edmonton. They were hosting teams from such countries as Korea, Japan, teams from the college circuit in the United States, Cuba and Mexico. It was truly an international meet. I discovered to my amazement that a number of athletes representing Canada would be unable to return to university that September because they were spending the summer representing Canada in international amateur competition. Most of these young athletes were university students who worked during the summer in order to pay for their university tuition. They gave up their summer to represent Canada in this international competition that they were hosting in Edmonton.
In 1961, the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act was passed to promote, encourage and develop fitness and amateur sport in Canada. There are two program directorates that function chiefly through the provision of financial assistance to national sport and fitness oriented organizations in Canada. The first is Fitness Canada. It initiates and supports research programs and the development of instructional and promotional materials designed to increase public awareness of benefits of fitness. In 1984-85, a total of 86 national associations, special agencies and programs and 18 universities were allocated $7.7 million in federal funding in support of fitness related projects.
The second directorate is Sport Canada which provides funding and services to national sport bodies, amateur athletes, university researchers and sport scientists as well as other members of the sport community. It has an annual budget of some $50 million and is the major supplier of funds for Canadian sport.
Sport Canada funds and works closely with the 85 national sport organizations in Canada, which include the national sport governing bodies responsible for specific sports, arm's-

length agencies such as the Coaching Association of Canada, multi-sport agencies such as the Canadian Inter-university Athletic Union, and specialized agencies such as the Sport Medicine Council of Canada. Its focus is on high-performance sport and contributions to the preparation of Canada's athletes for major international competition. Sport Canada also has an important commitment to the development of a strong domestic sports system which provides general opportunities for Canadians to participate in competitive sport.
Contributions are made to all recognized national sport organizations. These NSOs are eligible to receive core funding assistance in the areas of association management, technical development and high performance sport.
In 1984-85, Sport Canada distributed a total of $35.5 million in financial contributions among its various client associations. National sport organizations are voluntary organizations that are responsible for the development of their respective sport disciplines within Canada and for the preparation of high performance athletes and teams representing Canada in international competition. These are broken down into three groups, and this is where I believe Canada is falling behind. The first group is 27 sports on the 1988 Olympic Summer Games calendar. Those athletes involved in those sports who have A, B, or C carded athlete status are eligible for funds to help maintain the standard of living and continue their education while preparing for that sport. The second group includes 10 winter sports that will be featured at the Calgary Games.
Finally, there are 21 non-olympic disciplines. These include football, curling, free-style skiing, softball, baseball, raquet-ball, rugby, Canada five-pin and Canada ten-pin bowling, white water canoeing, karate, cricket, water skiing, squash, ringette, golf, lacrosse, parachuting, four-wall handball and soaring. Disabled sports are also included in this group.
Athletes participating in these sports are not recognized as athletes for A, B or C card purposes. One can only apply for this status when specifically recommended and can only be eligible for carded status after consideration by a review committee. In most cases these athletes are not eligible for carded athlete status whether or not they represent Canada in an international competition.
For example, those young amateur baseball players who hosted an international tournament in Edmonton last summer were not eligible for any assistance over and above their travelling expenses, accommodation and some pin money. Some of them had to give up a year of university in order to work and earn the money they would have earned during the summer they represented Canada on a national team.
In 1984-85, over $13 million was provided in core funding for the summer Olympic sports. The 10 winter Olympic sports received approximately $5 million in "best ever" programs and an additional $4 million in core contributions. Recent additions to the Olympic sports group include rhythmic gymnastics and synchronized swimming which were added to the 1984 Olympics. Prior to that, can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the young ladies who participated in the synchro swimming, and

the young ladies and young men who participated in rhythmic gymnastics were not supported in any way by their Government other than through the amateur sports councils until those sports were recognized. We know there were a lot of international meets, particularly in synchronized swimming. These young ladies had to spend all of their extra time and their summer months preparing for those meets. They had to have financial support from their families or they could not participate, and that is a shame.
I have tried to add up all the non-olympic sports where young Canadians would be involved in international competition and did not receive funding to continue with school. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to participate in this debate, although I had not intended to speak on this important issue. I do agree with the Hon. Member who put the motion that this is an issue that should be discussed before a committee.
I think there are a number of young athletes who are prevented from participating at the international level or from pursuing scholastic endeavours as a result of the current discriminatory nature which permits funding only of those sports recognized as Olympic designated sports. I think about roller skating. One of the world champions in roller skating came from my own community of Hamilton.
I have some concerns about the specific wording of the motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of awarding educational bursaries to members of teams who represent Canada at the amateur level in international competitions.
I would like to see this issue dealt with in greater detail in committee because I think there is a slight danger in introducing the notion of educational bursaries into the question of funding at an international level, which suggests athletes and students are necessarily synonymous. That is not always the case in international competition. There may be a number of young athletes who of their own choice or for other reasons have not decided to pursue post-secondary education and who are out in the workforce in the normal way.

February 11, 1986
Educational Bursaries
This motion while it would obviously respond to the needs of students pursuing athletic endeavours on the side would not respond adequately to those people who are pursuing an athletic endeavour in holding down a full-time job at the same time.
My second concern deals with the notion of introducing a kind of bursary system at the post-secondary level which is directed to those who participate in sports. I think we have seen in the United States very adequate evidence to show that often the quality of education or the quality of scholarship decreases as the level of participation in sports increases. This is not always the case and we have many fine athletes who have been able to combine academia and athletics. We also have a situation where athletes are encouraged to go to university. They get degrees in basket weaving and other creative endeavours at the university or post-secondary level in the United States, all the while using that particular bursary as a vehicle to pursue a sports endeavour.
I think it is pretty clear that in Canada, because we have tended to stay away from specific sports targeted bursaries for post-secondary education, we have been able to avoid the trap into which many universities and colleges in the United States have fallen. I think particularly of the college football system in the U.S. In a number of colleges and universities, coaches in particular have so abused the process that some of them have actually been forced out of their particular conferences and divisions. They have abused the process to the point where bursaries led to pay offs and to other under-the-table apportionments to encourage the various football players to go to a specific university.
If you are talking college football, Mr. Speaker, in the United States it is a very serious business indeed. Often the question of scholarship falls by the wayside. That is why I have some concerns about a motion that would tie the question of international competition to the issue of educational bursaries.
Certainly the Member has raised a very valid point about the financial prohibition that is, in essence, placed on those athletes who want to compete internationally, but I think it would be more effective if the Member dealt with that as a specific issue.
The notion of introducing educational bursaries for athletes at a time when transfer payments that the federal Government directs toward provincial Governments across the country are seeing a reduced number of dollars being put into them for the purpose of post-secondary education, would make it pretty difficult for those same universities to then swallow a program where we were directing larger sums of money toward bursaries for specifically designated athletes. That is why I think we should keep the question of athletics and scholarships, two questions, separate and apart.
I believe the merit of the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields), which is essentially to provide some kind of a vehicle for international competition, is valid. It does merit further consideration in a committee setting.
I would, however, reinforce my concern about specifically tying educational bursaries to athletic records. I think that in Canada we have been lucky not to have fallen into the kind of trap of absolute non-academia that we have seen in the United States. We would not like to see our colleges and universities here swamped with so-called scholars who have no business being there. That is the possible sequitor that would result from the adoption of a motion where educational bursaries would be presented to members of teams who represent Canada at amateur level in international competitions. It may inversely force athletes to go back to school when really they have no business or should not or choose not to be there simply because they want to have the funding to be able to carry on their athletic endeavours.
Rather than tying the two together the question is funding for athletes. What we should be looking at rather is a motion that would permit those athletes currently operating in nonolympic designated sports at the international level, which includes roller skating and a number of sports cited by the Hon. Member, to have access to the same level or similar levels of government funding for international competition as are currently available to our Olympic participants.
I know there are a number of sports that are trying and that have tried for a number of years to be recognized as Olympic sports. Obviously participants in these very valid and effective sports are being cutoff from Government funding because they have not been included in the rostrum of accepted and recognized Olympic sports.
While I support the spirit of the motion, I do have some reservations. I would be very happy to see the matter go into committee.

Sport Canada receives its mandate from the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act of 1961. Let me refer to that Act wherein it is indicated that it is to promote, encourage and develop fitness and amateur sport in Canada. In the 25 years since the enactment of that Act, sport and fitness have become an integral part of the Canadian way of life. No longer need we fear that proverbial 60-year old Swede. I am sure that all of us saw joggers working up a sweat today during their lunch hour along the Rideau Canal and up here on the Hill. Canadians have become more conscious of fitness and of the importance of a balanced diet. Certainly fewer of us smoke than was the case 25 years ago.

Mr. Speaker, in passing, I would like to mention the Department's major contribution towards improving the general level of fitness in this country. We have all heard about "Participac-tion", and when I look around, I think we all need to get out and get some exercise. However, there are two points I would like to bring to your attention: first of all, the remarkable contribution of our amateur athletes to international sport; and second, the way they are supported in their endeavour by Sport Canada. As we see it, the two go together: individual effort and achievements at the amateur level must have our support if they are to be successful.
However, as is the case in all financing programs, a choice must be made, and we must decide how to support amateur sport in a way that is satisfactory to Canadians. What criteria are we to use? What kind of priorities must be established so that we can manoeuver within the budgetary restrictions we must live with today?
I have said this before and I repeat: Sport Canada's aim is above all to promote excellence in amateur sport. We all believe that Canadians want to help our amateur athletes achieve the highest possible performance levels. And we will always remember with pride our participation in the 1984 Olympic Games!

Who can forget the thrill of seeing Gaetan Boucher, Canada's greatest Winter Olympian at Sarajevo, with his powerful, gliding stride and gold medal winning speed on the speed skating oval?
