Canada's best Olympic showing ever.

I would like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to announce that one of my fellow citizens who is now in Tignes, France, won the most points for acrobatic skiing in the last few days. I am referring to Lloyd Langlois from Magog, in my riding, who is with two of his fellow Quebecers from Beauport Lake, the Laroche brothers. 1 am expecting more news from France, and even if they do not win the championship, I think I will be as proud as ever of what they achieved during the last few days.
Our international class athletes have worked very hard to reach this level of excellence and they have achieved remarkable results, for instance, at the Commonwealth Games, and also at various other world championships. These young people deserve our unqualified admiration for their good work and dedication to their sport. We must not forget that they often have to compete with representatives from other countries who are heavily subsidized in various ways by their governments.
Sport Canada also recognizes the importance of financial assistance, which should be given to our international-class amateur athletes on a firm and continuing basis, with sound long-term planning. That is how we will be able to maintain the performance of Canadian athletes at international levels. The results themselves are the best testimony to the soundness of this approach. In recent years, Canada has been gradually improving its international performance, which reached its peak at the 1984 Olympic Games.

If we are to maintain and improve on these achievements, we must spend our sports dollars on continuing to develop such excellence. We therefore must support excellence in our young, promising athletes as well as our international athletes at their peak.

To develop this high degree of excellence among our young athletes, Sport Canada subsidizes and is working very closely with 85 sports organizations, and it also provides special
subsidies to Canadian amateur athletes under the Athlete Assistance Program.

Which sports qualify? To qualify for funding, a sport must meet the following criteria: First, it must hold a world championship or a world level competition at least every two years. Second, it must have a year round training program for each athlete or team. Third, it must have a monitoring and evaluation program for each athlete, with monthly reporting to Sports Canada. Fourth, it must have a formal selection process for national teams with published rules and an appeal process. Finally, in the international sports category, its national team or individual athletes must compete in at least two international competitions with at least 20 participating countries each year.

Through the Athletic Assistance Program we now offer financial aid to levels A, B and C athletes. We now have about 140 A-level athletes, which means they rank among the world's eight best in their sports. One hundred and thirty other athletes are at level B, therefore among the sixteen best athletes worldwide. The other 540 under the AAP are at level C, which designates international class athletes likely to qualify for levels A or B. Monthly assistance to athletes amounts to $650 at level A, $560 at level B and $450 at level C.

All that is quite expensive! Still this kind of assistance is a must for our athletes and it is one of the reasons why Sports Canada has recently gained international recognition.

Sport Canada currently spends roughly 10 per cent of its annual budget, or about $4 million, through the AAP. The support services outlined above cost many millions more. The AAP has been very effective and in itself is, we feel, another factor in our international success. Let us not forget, however, the main factor. Living expenses and top quality back-up are not enough.
The dogged motivation, the determination to succeed, have to be credited to the athletes themselves. It is their dedication, their individual sacrifice, their many hours of hard work, that ultimately achieve international results. Excellence is not just a matter of a year or two or slapdash training. It is the result of many hours on the practice field from a very early age. Only in this way can bodies be honed to the highest levels of achievement.
We are not dealing only with bodies and it is an important principle that we also provide for the development of the minds of these young people. All of our elite student athletes are given free tuition at any recognized Canadian educational institution under the AAP. Sport Canada makes sure that our athletes prepare for a lifelong career because life does not stop after athletics. This provision of the Athlete Assistance Plan can serve to introduce another important aspect of the Sport Canada program, the close working relationship with the Canadian Inter-University Athletic Union or the CIAU. The Canadian Interuniversity Athletic Union-CIAU-is the main university sports organization in Canada and includes most Canadian universities. National university competitions in twelve sports are organized each year for the 45 CIAU-member universities: track and field, basketball, football, gymnastics, hockey, lawn hockey, wrestling, swimming, diving, soccer and volleyball. Co-operation between Sports Canada and CIAU enables accredited athletes to train while attending university. Sports Canada and CIAU co-operation also makes it possible for the student-athlete to meet the standards of the program and have access to the best in terms of coaches, training and support services. Canada has chosen to achieve athletic excellence by stessing peak performance of both body and mind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what is the situation concerning bursaries for athletes attending Canadian universities? Several universities have indicated that they are in favour of these programs. It is unfair that Canadian athletes should be tempted into going to universities South of the border where they often find better facilities and better conditions as far as scholarships are concerned. Why do they decide to attend universities outside their own country? It is getting increasingly clear that

they do so because they are being offered better scholarships. I need only mention our young hockey players who by the hundreds are being awarded scholarships in American universities every year.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize two points. First of all, within the limits of available funds, we feel that the Athlete Assistance Program is the best way to provide Canadian athletes with an education in a Canadian surrounding and make it possible, if they so desire, to develop as athletes on the Canadian Sports scene. We are all only too well aware of the abuses that have taken place in the United States. We do not want to follow that example. We therefore intend to continue our excellent working relationship with the CIAU and will continue to support our athletes through the AAP, co-operation with that organization.
Sport Canada seeks to encourage a balance between athletics and scholarly activity in the lives of our athletes. There must be a place for both academic and athletic excellence in their development. Sport at one end of the scale must carry as much weight as a subsequent career at the other end because, as we have already stated, life after athletics goes on. This is how we help our athletes prepare for both of these aspects of their lives. This is the Canadian way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to comment briefly on the motion put by our hon. friend to have the appropriate committee study the entire question of offering scholastic bursaries to amateur athletes. I believe the discussion merits looking into further. There is no one in the Chamber who would dispute the fact that when we talk about the sporting world and athletes, we find quite often that the unrecognized and valiant heroes in the community are amateur athletes. There are many Rockys in the country who perhaps do not have the training, resources and proper coaching that require the moral and financial support that we as a nation can offer.
Of course, there are pros and cons with respect to tying athletic programs to our educational institutions. That is why, rather than talk this motion out or simply ignore it, we should meet it head on and have a good solid debate so that we may hear from the two schools of thought on this matter and perhaps reach a consensus.
Back in 1980, representatives of various Canadian athletic associations initially approved the entire concept of a bursary for athletics and then rejected the idea of athletic scholarships. In 1981, the Ontario University Athletics Association and the Ontario Women's Inter-Collegiate Association announced a boycott of all national championships involving institutions offering first-party scholarships.
There has been an ongoing debate regarding whether or not we should offer scholarships to amateur athletes. There are those, arguing in favour of it, who claim that athletic awards are an acceptable and desirable practice when funded by Governments, corporations and schools. There are those who say that the primary objective of athletic awards is simply to upgrade the standard of competition. There are those who say that unless we begin to counter what is being offered in the United States, we will lose the cream of the crop of our athletes. They point to the fact that there are over 1,000 Canadian amateur athletes training in or attending universities in the United States at this moment.
On the other side of the ledger, there are those who claim that if we get into the areas the American universities and college systems have entered, then we will also have a litany of abuses including an over-emphasis on athletics at the expense of academic excellence, falsification of student records, federal investigations into fixings of games and so on. They believe that the recruiting of athletes and their subsidization are two totally independent concepts. They also point to the numerous
scandals in the United States where athletes are suing universities for failing to provide a reasonable education after their athletic careers have been long terminated. There is also a fear that universities can become sports factories, if you will, with athletes entering university programs only with a professional sports career in mind and coaches basing success on the number of athletes chosen for the professional ranks.
There are obviously two schools of thought on the issue. There is no one in this House who disagrees with the fact that we should be financially and morally sponsoring our amateur athletes, no matter in what field of endeavour they participate. The real question is: How do we financially aid and support these athletes? Should they be tied down to our educational institutions?
I feel it is fitting that this debate be looked at by parliamentarians. We realize that the athletic associations of Ontario and Quebec, for instance, are opposed to tying athletic performance to university scholarships. Eastern Canada and western Canada have also had a difference of opinion on the matter for their various reasons. Therefore, if there exists a divergence of opinion across the land, then what better place is there than the Parliament of Canada, which is representative of all regions, to focus on the issue? It is not only a federal issue, since we all realize that education falls within the parameters of the provincial Governments. I think the debate should start here. I think that the athletes, the coaches, the sponsors and the numerous volunteers involved in amateur athletics would certainly welcome the opportunity to come before the appropriate committee of this House and present their evidence both for and against.
We should also take a look at the status of amateur athletes right now. There are those who say that athletic performance should not be tied to academics. Yet, they seem prepared to put sporting, especially in the amateur ranks, in the hands of tobacco companies or beer companies. Of course, there are those who say that that is in conflict with the whole issue of training and health associated with sporting activities. So there is a divergence of opinion with respect to amateur sports.
It is high time for us to take a look at the issue in a very real way. We should applaud the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) who moved this motion. I do not think it should be defeated. I do not think it should be talked out or ignored. That would be the easy way out of an issue which should receive the attention of the House, and through this House the attention of sporting communities in the country. Let them in concert with Parliament set a direction, a vision, for amateur athletics. Let us not lose the momentum which this motion gives us. If it can perhaps trigger and instigate a debate, then perhaps once and for all the matter can be laid to rest. Let us be courageous and respectable enough to take a look at the issue in the context in which it should be looked at. With those remarks I resume my seat and look forward to seeing the motion referred to committee.

Adjournment Debate
medal, a silver and a bronze went to the amazing Anne Ottenbrite. Victor Davis shattered his own world record to win the gold medal in the men's 220-metre breaststroke. Cyclist Steve Bauer took a silver medal, as did boxers Willy DeWitt and Shawn O'Sullivan. The two fighters are continuing, and one is from the riding of my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). Ben Johnson won the bronze medal in the 100-metre dash; and the women's relay team took the silver in the 4 by 400 relay race.
The list goes on and on. I cannot begin to do justice to all the medal winners. Suffice it to say that their names are in the record books and that they have given Canadians a lasting sense of pride. The credit for these successes must clearly go to the athletes. However, I think all Canadians can take some satisfaction in knowing that our amateur athletic development programs are paying off handsomely.
Canada has made steady progress on the international amateur scene since the introduction of the Fitness and Amateur Sport Act in 1961. There is no reason to believe that we will not continue to march forward in the years ahead.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BROADCASTING OF SONG LAUDING SUICIDE
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BROADCASTING OF SONG LAUDING SUICIDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on three separate occasions last month I rose in the House to express my concern over the irresponsibility of the CBC in continuing to broadcast the song "What It's Like to be Dead", in which children expound the virtues of death. When I requested that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) intervene to ensure that this song would not be broadcast again, I was reminded of the constraining provisions in the Broadcasting Act which grant ultimate responsibility for program selection and content to the broadcaster.
I do recognize the need for an arm's length policy and support it. However, as a representative of the people, I feel that the CBC is ultimately responsible to Parliament and to the taxpayers of Canada. Without the taxpayer, there would be no CBC.
I suggest to Mr. Juneau, President of the CBC, that his officials must be more responsible in their choice of program-

February 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
ming. The song "What It's Like to be Dead" transcends the limits of acceptable broadcasting. Although I appreciate the satirical nature of the Frantics, I know that most Canadians believe that suicide, especially teenage suicide, is no joke nor a laughing matter. The fact that the issue of teenage suicide is satirized at all tells me that we as a society do not comprehend the gravity and scope of this modern social problem.
Do we hear comedy troupes satirize wife beating or child sexual abuse on prime time radio? These are issues which Canadians have come to accept as being serious, serious enough that Governments and social agencies have effectively implemented programs to deal with the problem. I believe that the issue of teenage suicide should be treated in a similar fashion and not as a subject of tasteless humour. When I first started investigating the issue of teenage suicide, I was unaware of the size of the problem and its far-reaching effects on the families and friends of the victims. I decided to investigate speeches in Hansard of past Parliaments. I found to my amazement there has been no substantive debate on this issue since 1970s. As Parliamentarians, can we not let teenage suicide become the taboo of the 1980s, relegating it to the closet and pretending it doesn't exist. It does exist and it is a problem.
Let us consider some of the alarming statistics. Teenage suicide is up 400 per cent since 1970. Suicide is the leading cause of death among teenagers in Canada. More Canadians take their own life than die from either diabetes or sclerosis of the liver. Canadians are more likely to commit suicide than Americans. Research shows that of the people who commit suicide only 5 per cent have a history of mental illness. The Quebec Suicide Prevention Centre estimates that the suicide rate could be 10 per cent to 15 per cent higher when "doubtful" accidents are taken into account.
Literature on suicide too often focuses on the symptoms and statistics without mentioning the thoughts and feelings of young people who are locked into depression, who are devastated by the loss of a girlfriend or boyfriend, or peer or school pressures. The vast majority of suicidal teenagers feel that their parents and their elders do not understand or appreciate them. Adults tend to view teenage problems as little problems which will go away. It has been said that acne, sexual behaviour, school grades and career choices make it tough enough to be a teenager. On top of that there is a whole new set of pressures facing kids today at the next fragile stage of their lives.
The question remains if there is a problem, what do we do about it? Dr. Dianne Soyer-Solush of the Toronto East General made the following recommendations in a recent report on suicide in Canada: First, to introduce suicide prevention programs in public schools, as is presently done in three American states; second, that courses on suicide and suicide prevention be a mandatory part of physicians' training; third, that national standards be established for crisis centres across Canada. The time has come that we recognize the problem of teenage suicide and deal with it.
Mr. Juneau states, with regard to my complaint: "We would certainly never broadcast material which did constitute such an invitation because all of us recognize that teenage suicide is a terrible thing". I only wish he believed that statement. If he believes it, why would he, in a recent letter to me, condone broadcasting of this song without at least seeking some professional advise or, as I did? As a Government we must be committed, not only to inform people about this problem, but to set aside scarce resources from our Budget to ensure that our actions are effective.
In closing, I support the arms-length principle but, because of it, broadcasters must be more responsible in screening the content of their programming. Radio and TV are powerful mediums. They can alter people's attitudes and perceptions on this and many other issues. The public airwaves should be used responsibly for the good of the people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BROADCASTING OF SONG LAUDING SUICIDE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock) has raised a sensitive issue and we are all, I am sure, appreciative of his concern over the broadcast of the song "Neat to be Dead" on the CBC.
However, I would like to reiterate what the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) emphasized previously in the House, that is, that broadcasters themselves are responsible for program selection and content subject to the general rules and regulations of the CRTC. Consequently, responsibility for CBC programming matters lies entirely with the CBC's management and board of directors. The Minister of Communications has no direct power of intervention in such matters.
Neither I nor the Minister, and I am sure no Hon. Members, would wish to set the potentially dangerous precedent of restricting the CBC's right to programming autonomy by becoming directly involved in this particular programming matter, as sensitive as it is. Moreover, the Minister assured the House that he would inform both the CBC and the CRTC of the concern about the song "Neat to be Dead" which was expressed in the House. I was pleased to hear that Mr. Juneau responded, although the response was not entirely satisfactory.
I learned, Mr. Speaker, during a recent visit of Finnish parliamentarians to Parliament Hill that one of the regulations within the Finnish broadcasting system prohibits programming which might be injurious to mental health. I do not know whether that sort of regulation would be useful, or whether the CRTC would want to address it. On the other hand, I heard the Hon. Member say that only 5 per cent of those who commit suicide are believed to be suffering from mental illness.
The Hon. Member has certainly underscored the sensitivity of the topic matter and the Minister appreciates his concern. However, Mr. Speaker, I would like us to keep in mind the democratic principle of freedom of expression. The Charter of Rights guarantees freedom of expression for Canadians and the Broadcasting Act itself states clearly: " . .. the right to freedom of expression and the right of persons to receive
February 11, 1986

programs, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations, is unquestioned".
Mr. Speaker, having been myself in broadcasting, I can tell this House that decision-making on programming is often a difficult process which involves trying to offer programs which will be as attractive, exciting, dramatic or humourous as the public demands or finds acceptable. It is not always easy to ensure that a specific program will offend no one. If a program makes part of the audience uneasy or is found to be in bad taste, it is certainly not what the broadcasters wanted. After all, Mr. Speaker, whether they are public or private, broadcasters must answer the questions of their audience.
Mr. Speaker, all broadcasters, and I speak from experience, treat their programming responsibilities with respect and with an eye to the future. I am not speaking only about the programs themselves, but also about public reactions to these programs. I believe that the CBC is seriously considering the issue raised by the Hon. Member and that, in so doing, it is taking its responsibilties very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising today to discuss a question asked on January 20 during the Question Period to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens).
My question relates to the report of the Textiles and Clothing Commission and the various comments which I have read or heard recently. I also want to make a few points in this regard.
Over one year ago, on January 30, 1985, I informed the House that the crisis in the textile and clothing industry had continued and worsened for then years because of the massive imports from low-wage semi-industrialized Pacific rim countries.
In its last report published in late December, the Commission states that, during the period from 1972 to 1982, 31,977 jobs were lost in Canada.
Most of these jobs were in Quebec. The Commission also blamed the Liberal Government for not having implemented its recommendations.
On page 84 of its report, the Commission says that the Liberals ignored its recommendation that existing agreements and quotas be extended until the end of 1990.
A new Federal textile policy should contain reference to the fact that imports are not to increase by 13 per cent a year, as in the last four years, when the market increases only by 1.5 per cent a year, and it should be modelled on clause 3 of the
Adjournment Debate
Multifibre Agreement, as is the policy of the European Economic Community to regulate imports.
I also take the liberty of suggesting to the Minister that he should include leather garments in the next agreements, as suggested by the report, and that any unused quotas should be eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, you will know that according to a Quebec Government study, in Quebec only, 30,000 jobs would be lost in the textile and clothing industries, were free to arranged with the United States.
It must also be emphasized that the textile and clothing industries are interrelated, because the clothing industry accounts for 40 per cent of the textile industry's market.
Incidentally, CIRB's Chairman, Mr. Tsai, mentioned last week in the Board's fourth and most recent annual report that it will have committed $267 million during its mandate.
The Industrial and Commercial Development Program is the second feature of CIRB's mandate, and its goal is to consolidate and diversify the economies of areas that are strongly dependent on the textile, clothing and footwear industries. The subsidized companies will invest a total of $358.4 million, including $97.1 million in contributions from the Industrial and Commercial Development Program. CIRB's contributions that have been approved since the inception of the program should help create 4,834 direct jobs, 672 of which would be in Drummondville.
Also, in 1984-85, restructuring plans for 100 businesses have been approved representing $134.1 million in investments with $39.4 million in financial help from the CIRB.
The textile industry is doing its share in the area of modernization, with respect to technology as well as management and creativity. Let me remind you that over the last decade, upwards of $2 billion have been invested with the purpose in mind. The industry is asking that the multifiber arrangement be implemented with more firmness and closer monitoring. This objective, coupled with a wiser use of macro-economic policies, will enable the private sector to plan and invest with confidence.
In my constituency, people are striving to find solutions for improving productivity in the textile industry genrally. Indeed, constituents of mine have take the initiative of requesting a feasibility study for a center for applied research in textiles. Also, constituents of mine are now doing that survey with a sampling of 200 industries. It must be hoped that such a project well not be doomed by improper decisions, as was the case under the previous administration.
Further more, I would like the Minister to consider imposing an overall quota on imports from all countries, under section XIX of the GATT.
Should there be further plant shutdowns, think of the cost of retraining those workers under the Labour Adjustment Ben-

February 11, 1986
Adjournment Debate
efits Program. It should be said that subsidies are given to grain, milk and red meat producers because those products are considered necessities of life. Then, we could very well subsidize clothing which is also a necessity.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would humbly submit to the Minister a proposal to include in the long term plan he was referring to on November 29, 1984, one aspect that the inquiry failed to mention, namely a labelling policy that might inform consumers as to the nature of the product and the origin of the garmen they are purchasing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I would like to answer a question by the Hon. Member for Drummond (Mr. Guilbault) concerning the implementation of recommendations made by the Textile and Clothing Board.
Mr. Speaker, first of all I can assure my hon. friend that the Government is fully aware of the importance of the textile and clothing industry for the Canadian economy, and especially for the economy of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Nova Scotia. In fact, one or both of these sectors are represented to some extent in all our provinces. Textile and clothing ranks second in Canada in the manufacturing sector, after food and beverages, and provides direct employment for
172,000	workers, while shipping products estimated at more than $10.5 billion. Quebec alone has over 96,000 workers in this sector. The clothing industry is concentrated in Montreal, where it represents 24 per cent of all manufacturing jobs. Many other Quebec communities, including the riding of Drummond, depend to a large extent on the textile and clothing industry. The clothing sector is also of considerable importance for Winnipeg, where it represents 17 per cent of all jobs in the manufacturing sector.
Considering the very substantial contribution of the textile and clothing sector to our national and regional economies, the Government has committed itself to maintaining a viable textile and clothing industry in Canada. To do so, the Ministers responsible have met several times with representatives from both industries to discuss the negative impact of the sudden rise in clothing imports from countries with low production costs that occurred in 1983 and 1984.
In addition the Textile and Clothing Board was asked to carry out an exhaustive investigation in the situation of those two industries, and it eventually made public the report mentioned by the Hon. Member.
The main conclusion of the TCB report is that imports from countries where wages are low or where industries are government-supported are causing serious damage to Canadian producers and that the situation can only get worse in the future. This situation can be explained by the fact that the clothing
industry is labour-intensive and that our workers are much better paid than those of Asia, South America and Africa.
The main recommendations of the report are aimed at improving Canada's import restriction system within the multifibre agreement to which our country is signatory. As my colleague pointed out, this agreement is due to expire at the end of July this year. But we expect it will be renewed. It provides for negotiations between importing and exporting countries to arrive at bilateral textile and clothing agreements with which both parties can live. speechtext:
Thank you for setting me straight, Mr. Speaker. I always appreciate your guidance.
It is a sad duty for me to raise in this forum the question of the developing machines marketed by the now notorious Key Independent Systems in Canada. It arises out of my question in the House on November 29, 1985, concerning the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, although the Minister was not present at the time and 1 had given advance notice of my question. The answer which I received from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) was that the Minister would get back to me with a response. Indeed that happened, but not in any way which I could deem satisfactory or not in any way which shed any light on this very sorry story of the swatch which the company had cut through independent businesses in Canada and the damage which has been done, not only to its own reputation but to individual entrepreneurs in several parts of the country.
The response which I received from the Minister just five days later indicated that the matter was under examination and that it would be inappropriate to comment further. At this time it is very appropriate to comment further because it is now the second anniversary of the information, as I understand it, being laid which led to the initiation of the investigation by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs of the operation of Key Independent Systems and its financial part-
February 11, 1986

ners in the retailing of these machines, namely, the financial subsidiary of Societe generate, one of the largest banks in France. Perhaps unfortunately for some of my own theories it is now effectively under the control of the French Government.
The history has been a long, sorry one, and that is why I feel it is incumbent upon the Parliamentary Secretary to let the House know, as we are all eagerly awaiting it, the action which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) has taken and will be taking.
It appears that as a result of the non-performance of these machines, which were marketed with guarantees and with promises of performance that were glowing and which have now turned out to be extravagant and even false, approximately 40 businessmen in Canada have gone bankrupt. I think that it is sad, a tragedy which is deserving of Government examination, and certainly deserving of government intervention. Indeed, the aggrieved owners and former owners of these machines have formed an association. They have an executive director. That is surely an indication of the damage that was done. It was stated in a letter from the Solicitor General (Mr. Beatty), that KIS advertised that a company developing 30 rolls of film a day would reap $100,000 a year in profits. A London, Ontario company which averaged 29 rolls a day is now bankrupt. I could go on, although I do not want to use up the time that way. There are several similar examples of people who did their utmost to keep these machines working, replacing defective parts with higher grade materials, following all the service recommendations and instituting additional preventive and restorative maintenance of their own, but who still could not get anything like the performance out of these machines that Key Independent Systems was promising.
There are further marketing scandals related to that company. It has apparently been marketing a key-cutting machine in Ontario, which Ontario Hydro has not approved for connection to the provincial electric utility. It has apparently been bringing in used machines from the United States for sale in Canada as if they were new. We know that the financing contracts were sold instantly by the company to Societe gene-rale, the finance subsidiary. It appears from the statements by the Ontario KIS owners association that-through what means we do not know-somehow this company has been replacing its Canadian personnel with personnel imported from France. That is something that the Government, although it does not fall within the purview of the responsibility of this particular Ministry, should be concerned about.
The lending practices of this financial subsidiary should be investigated. Apparently there was some guaranteed agreement between the finance subsidiary and the parent, Societe generale and the KIS company in France, that forced the financing company to finance these machines, thus effectively interposing a third party-who presumably acted in good faith though not with the best of judgment-into the deal between KIS systems and the Canadian independent businessmen who were still using those machines. What is even stranger and
Adjournment Debate
even more worthy of attention by the Government is that once the original investigation had started, it was found that there was nothing in the legislation that could be used to stop either the financing or the sales practices of this particular company. Those are the questions I would like to put to the Parliamentary Secretary, and those are the questions to which many small-businessmen and women deserve answers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Domm), I have been asked to respond on his behalf to the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rai-ny River (Mr. Parry) and to the concerns expressed by other Hon. Members regarding this matter.
KIS Minute Canada sold a number of photo-developing machines to business people across Canada which were purported to be capable of processing a certain number of films in a given time. Many of these businesses were dissatisfied with the equipment sold to them and have indicated to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and to the media, that poor service for the equipment and machinery malfunctions prevented them from achieving the capacity of the equipment claimed by the company. Many of these purchasers have formed KIS owner associations and are actively pursuing redress through civil litigation and other means. The company maintains that the equipment can produce at its rated capacity and has identified KIS owners who are satisfied with the equipment.
The Department is also aware of complaints by KIS owners alleging that there was improper use of testimonials by the company, and that sales representatives of the company have misrepresented the earning potential of the machines. The Director of Investigation and Research under the Combines Investigation Act is examining these allegations in relation to the misleading advertising provisions of the Act. As you know, the confidentiality provisions of the statute prevent the disclosure of information related to the consideration of such matters. Accordingly, it would be inappropriate for me to comment on the nature or progress of the director's examination. However, I can indicate that at the conclusion of any inquiry, the director may refer the matter under Section 15(1) of the Act to the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Crosbie). It is he who determines whether or not charges should be laid.
The Hon. Member should bear in mind, however, that if a prosecution were to ensue, it would take place before the criminal courts. Consequently, each element of an offence would have to be established beyond a reasonable doubt. This requirement can place a difficult burden on the conduct of inquiries.
I can also state that Departmental officials have met with some of the complainants to review their concerns. I can assure the House that the matter is receiving a careful and complete examination of all the facts available. Should charges be laid

against KIS Minute Canada or its principals, the Minister will be pleased to inform Hon. Members.
